item.title: Spark Program | Sigsheet: a unified standard for signing CKB multisig transactions
item.dc:creator: ILE_LABS
item.description:
Applicant: ILE Labs

Funding requested: $2,000 USD

Duration: 7 weeks, starting at approval (the first payment)

Payout address: ckb1qyqpkgfq00mzpsqh4e4gxpkdh3nafsepvl0qpddkyy

Contact: contact@ilelabs.org, Discord: emmzy_code01

In our own words

Our first application, ckb-msig, converted signatures between the formats CKB wallets already write. The committee’s answer was clear: instead of adapting to the fragmentation, design the standard that every tool can adopt. So that’s what we did. Sigsheet is one file and one set of rules for a CKB multisig transaction, and the specification draft, its test vectors and an independent check are already public. This grant turns the draft into a standard wallets can adopt: two libraries that implement it, in TypeScript and Rust, one tool that lets today’s ckb-cli and Neuron users sign while their wallets catch up, and a demo on testnet across all three tools.

1. Project Overview

What it is. Sigsheet is an open standard for signing a CKB multisig transaction: one canonical JSON file per transaction, and the rules every tool follows to read, check, sign, merge and finalize it. It’s what the committee asked for in its reply to our first application (t/11151 #2): “a unified standard for multisig signature formats — one that ckb-cli, Neuron, CCC, and other tools would collectively adopt.”

How wallets adopt it. Two libraries implement the whole standard and pass the same test vectors: TypeScript, for CCC apps and Neuron, and Rust, for ckb-cli and other Rust tools. A wallet adds one of them and signs with its own signer and keys. Its users can then co-sign with users of every other wallet that reads the file. Until a wallet does, one Sigsheet tool lets its users sign with the wallet as it is (section 4.4).

What it does for signers. Each signer uses the wallet they already have. Signatures are kept per lock group and per signer, so anyone can merge copies, in any order, with the same result, and nobody has to collect them. When enough members have signed, anyone finalizes the file into a standard CKB transaction.

Who it’s for:

  • groups whose members sign the same multisig with different tools: ckb-cli, Neuron or an app built on CCC;
  • payout signers, team treasuries and contract upgrades (section 3.2);
  • wallet and app developers, who get one tested format to support instead of one per tool, and a library that does the work (section 4.2).

At a glance:

  • Name: Sigsheet
  • Type: an open standard with open-source implementations (MIT)
  • Repository: ILE-Labs/Sigsheet, with the specification draft and the research behind it
  • Discussion: t/11298 on Nervos Talk
  • Duration: 7 weeks, one milestone a week
  • Phase: v0.1. v0.2 and v1.0 are open milestones (section 11).

2. Team Profile

ILE Labs builds open-source tools for CKB. For Sigsheet we:

  • wrote the specification draft and its 44 test vectors;
  • built the generator that rebuilds every vector byte for byte, and an independent check against CCC’s, ckb-cli’s and ckb-sdk’s own code and the deployed lock binaries;
  • tested today’s signing flows in ckb-cli, Neuron and CCC, and recorded every result on the research branch.

Everything, including this application’s milestones and issues, is public in ILE-Labs/Sigsheet.

3. Background

3.1 The problem

A CKB multisig transaction is signed by several people, often with different tools. Every tool and project that handles a partly signed multisig transaction keeps it in its own way. Our research (sections 4 to 6, and 11) has the details:

Tool or project How it keeps a partly signed multisig transaction
ckb-cli Its tx file, with the signatures keyed by lock args and no input cells, so it needs a node. Contract deployments use a separate deploy file
Neuron Its offline-signing file: the signatures are appended in the witness, and who has signed is in a map keyed by lock hash
CCC, and every app built on it No file: the signatures live in the transaction’s witness, in slots of a fixed length
ckb-sdk (Rust) No file: its signer puts each signature in the first empty slot of the witness
UTXO Global’s multisig wallet Its own server. Signing goes through one wallet, its own (website), and only the 2024 deployment is supported (server constants)
.bit’s signing site ckb-cli files only: “Invalid transaction data, only ckb-cli format is supported.” (ckb-multisig-wizard)
kuai “Currently kuai deployment contract only supports local signature deployment, which is a very bad experience when using multiple devices for multi-signature.” (kuai#276)
ChainPay Its own coordinator: “ChainPay coordinates partial signatures.” (chain-pay)
A 2024 proof of concept It converted ckb-cli and Neuron files, for the genesis deployment only. Its last commit was 2024-03-05 (ckb-multisig-cobuild-poc)
Two earlier shared formats An offline-signing draft (t/5794, 2021) and CKB Open Transaction (rfcs#406, closed unmerged). Neither became a standard

So signatures don’t move between tools. Both of these were measured in X1:

  • ckb-cli to Neuron. The incompatibility was reported in 2024 (neuron#3048), and Neuron added an import (#3169). But with Neuron v0.204.1’s own code, importing a ckb-cli file that held two signatures gave signatures: {}.
  • Neuron to CCC. CCC reads Neuron’s exported transaction, but turns its witness into 0x, which loses the partial signature.

So in practice:

  • one person collects the signatures from chat, PR comments or files, checks them by eye and assembles the transaction;
  • signers can’t check what they sign offline, from one file;
  • no tool covers all three multisig deployments. ckb-cli and Neuron don’t sign the 2024 deployment (design record, section 8.2, test 5). Its lock held 4,935,609.54 CKB in 93 live cells at block 21,098,567 (measured on 2026-11-24 with get_cells_capacity on a public mainnet node).

The problem isn’t making signatures. It’s making them portable, checkable and mergeable between tools.

3.2 Evidence of demand

The full list, with every quote, is on the evidence branch of our first project. These are the main ones.

Payouts take days or weeks.

  • A DAO payout (2-of-3) was started on Aug 21 and completed on Sept 4. In zz_tovarishch’s words, t/10583/20: “一位委员会成员在 8月21 该项目通过投票后，以2500/$0.00087= 2,873,564 CKB 发起了打款，随后在 9.4 其他委员会成员才完成了多签”. Translated: a committee member started the payment on Aug 21, after the vote, and only on Sept 4 did the other members complete the multisig.
  • The DAO said the same in 2024. JackyLHH, t/7849/1: “This is because DAO’s funds are stored in a multisig wallet, so it takes some time to collect signatures due to timezone and other factors.”
  • Spark pays every grant from a multisig (t/8752).

Contract upgrades run through PR comments. For Fiber’s v0.7.0 mainnet upgrade (fiber-scripts#34, 3-of-5), each signer ran ckb-cli deploy sign-txs and pasted the output into a comment, for one person to check and merge. v0.1 works on the transactions ckb-cli, CCC apps and Neuron build, not yet on ckb-cli’s deploy files.

Core developers asked for it.

  • doitian, ckb-cli#603: “Help users to prepare files for requesting multisig signatures from signers. Generate the tx json file and a markdown guidance for signers.”
  • doitian, ckb-cli#569: “It’s frustrated that sign-txs does not tell how to use the generated signatures”

Teams keep building their own: .bit’s signing site, kuai and ChainPay, in the table in section 3.1.

Neuron users get stuck.

  • jordanmack, neuron#2907: “I tried to send and I can’t figure out how to sign and broadcast.”
  • rink1969, neuron#3260: offline multisig on a transaction that mixed locks ended with “报签名失败” (translated: signing failed).

Bitcoin solved this with one shared format. PSBT (BIP-174) “holds the signatures for an input while the input does not have a complete set of signatures”, and wallets interoperate through it. CKB has no such standard. Sigsheet is that standard for CKB.

3.3 What changed since our first application

The committee gave two reasons (t/11151 #2), and this is how Sigsheet answers each:

  1. “signers must still collect all signatures and forward them to a single individual for aggregation”. In Sigsheet there’s no collector role. The file passes from signer to signer, or each signer posts a copy and anyone merges the copies, with the same result in any order. In v0.1 each signer still receives the file and passes it on, so the coordinating is reduced, not removed (design record, section 10). v0.2’s optional relay carries one signature at a time, so wallets can deliver them automatically.
  2. “design and propose a unified standard for multisig signature formats”. That’s Sigsheet: a public specification with test vectors, not a converter. ckb-msig adapted to each tool’s format. Sigsheet gives every tool one format to read and write, and two libraries to adopt it with.

4. Solution

4.1 The standard

A Sigsheet file carries everything a signer needs to check what they sign, offline and from the file alone (spec, section 1):

  • the unsigned transaction, and the witness templates of its lock groups;
  • every previous transaction its inputs spend, so each input cell is checked by hash;
  • the headers and inclusion proofs a Nervos DAO withdrawal needs;
  • the multisig configs;
  • every signature so far, keyed by lock group and signer.

The rules every implementation follows:

  • one canonical form (RFC 8785), so the same file has the same bytes everywhere;
  • 31 reader checks, so every tool refuses the same bad files;
  • a lock’s kind comes from the chain, never from the file: the code hash and hash type of the cell it spends (spec, section 6.1);
  • each lock’s own signing message, computed from the file alone;
  • a merge that gives the same bytes in any order, and a finalize that writes the standard transaction;
  • the three multisig deployments (genesis, 2024 and v2) and the single-key lock. New lock kinds are added without a format change (spec, section 12).

The final transaction uses the existing CKB locks. Sigsheet needs no new on-chain script and no change to existing multisig addresses.

4.2 How a wallet adopts it, and why it would

How. A wallet adds Sigsheet with one of the two libraries. The languages match the main CKB tools: TypeScript, on @ckb-ccc/core, for CCC apps and Neuron; Rust for ckb-cli and other Rust tools. Then:

  1. Open a Sigsheet. The library reads the file and runs every check.
  2. Show the signer what they’re signing, derived from the checked data: the outputs, the inputs and their cells, and each group with its members.
  3. Sign with the wallet’s own signer. The library gives the wallet each group’s signing message. The wallet signs it the way it signs today, with its own keys, and the library adds the signature. Keys never leave the wallet.
  4. Share it. Merge copies, and finalize once enough members have signed.
  5. Prove it. Run the 44 test vectors. Passing them means the wallet gives the same bytes as every other implementation.

At design stage, adding Sigsheet inside each wallet was a small change. It took 381 code lines in ckb-cli (plus 87 for creating a file), 229 in CCC and 137 in Neuron, and each wallet’s own tests gave the same results before and after (X6).

It works with CCC as it is. The TypeScript library is its own package on @ckb-ccc/core as published, so any CCC app can add it today, with nothing to merge into CCC and nothing to wait for. That’s where it sits after our discussion with CCC’s maintainer on ccc#646.

Why a wallet would adopt it:

  • Its users can sign with everyone else’s. One format means a wallet’s users co-sign with the users of every other wallet that reads it, with no converter for each pair of wallets.
  • The hard parts come done. The canonical form, the 31 reader checks, the 18 attack cases, Nervos DAO withdrawals and the three multisig deployments are all specified and covered by the test vectors. A wallet doesn’t design or maintain any of it.
  • Its signers can check what they sign, offline. The file carries every previous transaction, so the wallet can show each input cell without trusting a node.
  • It keeps its own signing. The wallet signs with its own code and keys. The standard only fixes what the message is.
  • It’s small and open. The change was small at design stage (above), the specification and the libraries are MIT, and nothing is hosted.
  • The interim tool steps aside. Once a wallet reads Sigsheet itself, its users don’t need the Sigsheet tool.

4.3 How it’s used

  1. A signer’s tool creates a Sigsheet for a multisig transaction.
  2. Each signer’s tool reads the file and runs the checks.
  3. The signer reviews what the transaction does, and signs their group with their own wallet.
  4. The signed file is passed on, or posted as a copy.
  5. Anyone merges the copies. Any order gives the same file.
  6. When enough members have signed, anyone finalizes it into the transaction to send.

4.4 Until wallets adopt it: the Sigsheet tool

Nothing in v0.1 waits for any wallet’s maintainers. Apps built on CCC sign with the TypeScript library directly. For the wallets that don’t read Sigsheet yet, one Sigsheet tool opens the file, checks it, and shows what’s being signed. Then it gets the signature from the signer’s own wallet, through that wallet’s own file: the official Neuron through its offline-signing file (neuron#3518), and the official ckb-cli through its tx file (ckb-cli#694). Neither wallet is changed, and no key passes through the tool.

  • What it adds: one step for those signers (sign in the wallet, then bring the signature back), which native support removes. ckb-cli’s signing reads the input cells from its node, as it does today.
  • Where today’s wallets fall short. The standard and both libraries handle these cases. The tool can only pass on what a wallet signs:
    • Neuron v0.204.1 leaves the witnesses beyond the inputs out of its signing message, so its signature on such a transaction doesn’t verify (X1). The tool holds those files back from Neuron signers, who sign them in ckb-cli or a CCC app instead, and we offer Neuron the fix as a pull request.
    • The official ckb-cli and Neuron don’t sign the 2024 deployment at all. Sigsheet’s libraries handle it, so a 2024 multisig is signed in a wallet or app that uses one, such as a CCC app with the TypeScript library.

It isn’t a bridge. Wallets don’t talk to each other through it. Every wallet writes to the same file, and anyone merges the copies. When a wallet adopts the standard, its signers don’t need the tool. The README’s questions explain why one file and one tool work where a bridge doesn’t.

4.5 Why a new format, not an existing one

We tested the alternatives before writing the spec (paths):

  • Converting between today’s formats is what ckb-msig did, and the committee asked for a standard instead.
  • Keeping partial signatures inside the transaction’s witness, as CCC does, depends on the order of the files.
    • Our test case was Fiber’s v0.7.0 upgrade, a 3-of-5 multisig with five signatures. Merging the five copies with CCC’s aggregateTransactions in all 120 orders always gave a valid multisig witness, but 60 different ones: it kept the first three signatures in file order.
    • The single-key input’s signature survived only in the 24 orders where its copy came first (X3a, section 1).
  • Sigsheet keeps each signature by lock group and signer until the end. That rule gave the same result in 2,000 of 2,000 design-stage trials (X3a, section 2).

5. What’s already built

The MVP is complete (milestone):

  • the specification’s first draft;
  • 44 test vectors: 24 cases, 18 attacks and 2 mainnet transactions. Each case holds the file as created, one copy per signature, the merged file, the final transaction and its expected results. Each attack says whether a reader must refuse it or drop its signatures;
  • the generator, which rebuilds every vector byte for byte;
  • an independent check: CCC’s, ckb-cli’s and ckb-sdk’s own code, and every final transaction run through the deployed lock binaries under ckb-debugger, with negative controls that must fail as the chain does;
  • the checks on Linux, macOS and Windows, on every pull request.

The research is on the research branch: the design record, the experiments, and the design-stage wallet patches and benchmarks.

The feedback so far:

  • The spec is open for comment in t/11298, and has been shared with ckb-cli’s and Neuron’s maintainers (ckb-cli#694, neuron#3518).
  • On ccc#646, CCC’s side found three problems, and we’ve accepted all three for v0.1:
    • the Nervos DAO deposit-header index is read two ways, by the DAO script and by the node’s fee calculation;
    • a merge can produce a file a reader refuses, by going past the 255-signature limit for a carried group;
    • the CoBuild profile’s round trip covers fewer files than the draft said.

6. What this grant pays for: seven weeks

Each week is a GitHub milestone, and each task is an issue with its own acceptance test.

Week Milestone Tasks
1 TypeScript reference implementation on CCC: read, check and show #9 read, check and show a file
2 TypeScript reference implementation on CCC: sign, merge, finalize, create and send #10 sign, merge and finalize; #11 create and send
3 Rust library: read, check and show #12 read, check and show a file
4 Rust library: sign, merge, finalize, create and send #13 sign, merge and finalize; #14 create and send
5 The Sigsheet tool, with the official ckb-cli and Neuron #16 sign in the official Neuron; #17 create a Sigsheet from Neuron’s export; #15 hold back files Neuron can’t sign, and offer Neuron the fix; #55 sign in the official ckb-cli, and create a Sigsheet from its tx file
6 Testnet demo with all three tools #18 each tool reads and signs the files the other two create; #19 the testnet demo, with every transaction hash published
7 Spec v0.1, the documentation, the benchmarks re-run and v0.1.0 #20 answer every comment and list the changes; #21 specification v0.1; #25 all ten acceptance tests in one command, and the benchmarks re-run; #52 the documentation; #26 the v0.1.0 tag

The testnet demo puts a 2-of-3 genesis multisig and a 3-of-5 v2 multisig on testnet, signed across the tools: once passed from signer to signer, and once posted as copies and merged by someone who isn’t a signer.

7. Required Funding and Breakdown

$2,000 in total, by week and task:

Week Task Cost
1 #9 read, check and show $170
2 #10 sign, merge and finalize $170
2 #11 create and send $110
3 #12 read, check and show $130
4 #13 sign, merge and finalize $150
4 #14 create and send $120
5 #16 sign in the official Neuron $110
5 #17 create from Neuron’s export $50
5 #15 hold back files Neuron can’t sign, and the fix for Neuron $60
5 #55 sign in the official ckb-cli, and create from its tx file $80
6 #18 the cross-tool record $200
6 #19 the testnet demo $150
7 #20 answer the feedback $50
7 #21 specification v0.1 $100

7 #52 the documentation $100
After v0.1.0 Six months of maintenance: a reply within 72 hours to issues and feedback, fixes to v0.1, dependency updates and documentation $150
Total $2,000

Why the weeks differ:

  • Week 1 ($170) is the reader of every rule: the canonical check, the 31 checks, the lock kinds taken from the chain, and what a signer is shown.
  • Week 2 ($280) completes the reference implementation: signing through CCC’s signers, the merge, ready and finalize, and creating and sending with a node. The Sigsheet tool is built on it.
  • Week 3 ($130) is the same reader in Rust, giving the same results as the TypeScript library on every vector.
  • Week 4 ($270) is signing through a signer the wallet provides, the merge and finalize in Rust, and creating and sending.
  • Week 5 ($300) is the Sigsheet tool, built on the TypeScript library. The work is the two wallets’ own files, reading their signatures back, and the fix offered to Neuron, with Neuron’s own tests.
  • Week 6 ($350) runs every pairing of the three tools on a devnet, then the testnet transactions.
  • Week 7 ($350) is the specification after the feedback, the ten acceptance tests in one command, and the documentation.

Why above $1,000. One standard that three tools, in two languages, must implement and check against shared test vectors, on the genesis, 2024 and v2 deployments. With $1,000 we’d build the two implementations (Weeks 1 to 4, $850) and stop there: no Sigsheet tool for ckb-cli and Neuron signers, no cross-tool testnet demo, and no specification v0.1 from the feedback.

Payment. 20% ($400) at approval. The rest in parts at the weekly check-ins, each a closed milestone with its results shown, or after completion.

8. Deliverables and How to Verify

Each week closes a milestone whose issues say how they’re verified. Most checks need no code reading:

  • Transactions: the testnet demo’s transactions are published with their hashes and the tool behind each signature, so any explorer shows them (test 8).
  • One command: a single command runs all ten acceptance tests (design record, section 8.2). The tests:
    • both implementations reproduce every vector byte for byte;
    • each attack is refused, or its signatures are dropped;
    • a merge in at least 200 random orders gives one result;
    • every check runs with networking off;
    • each tool reads and signs the files the other two create;
    • a genesis multisig with N ≥ 11 passes a node’s pool check;
    • each wallet’s own tests pass before and after its change;
    • the testnet transactions;
    • the feedback, with its list of changes;
    • the Nervos DAO case.
  • A record: for every pairing of tools, the files, their hashes and the committed devnet transactions are kept in the repository.

v0.1.0 is tagged only when all ten pass at that commit.

9. Maintenance

For six months after v0.1.0, ILE Labs maintains the release:

  • a reply within 72 hours to every new GitHub issue in the repository, and to every comment on this thread and on the spec thread (t/11298);
  • triage of reported issues;
  • fixes to v0.1;
  • corrections to checks or compatibility found in real use;
  • dependency updates;
  • the documentation and the test instructions.

This doesn’t promise new features. The repository stays open to contributions and review.

10. CKB Alignment

  • It builds on what CKB already has: the existing multisig and single-key locks on all three deployments, and the standard transaction, with no new on-chain script.
  • Adopting it is small, and stays in each wallet’s hands: a library, the wallet’s own signer, and the shared test vectors.
  • It’s meant to become a CKB standard. v1.0 is a stable specification with a conformance suite any implementation can run, proposed as a CKB RFC.
  • It helps the people who sign CKB’s shared funds: payout signers, team treasuries and contract upgraders, whatever tool each member uses.

11. After Spark: the roadmap

These are open milestones, published before this application:

  • v0.2:
    • a readable summary for signers;
    • a command that writes the file and that summary in one step, in the Sigsheet tool and offered to ckb-cli;
    • an optional relay that carries one signature at a time, about 367 bytes at design stage, instead of the whole file;
    • Omnilock’s multisig mode;
    • Neuron’s own Sigsheet screens, offered to Neuron as pull requests;
    • support in more tools.
  • v1.0: a stable specification with a conformance suite, proposed as a CKB RFC.

Questions we expect

Why would a wallet adopt Sigsheet, and how much work is it?

  • Why: its users can then co-sign with the users of every other wallet that reads the file. The checks, the attack cases, Nervos DAO withdrawals and the three deployments come specified and tested, and the wallet keeps its own signing and keys.
  • The work: one library, the wallet’s own signer, and the 44 test vectors to prove it. At design stage the change was 381 code lines in ckb-cli, 229 in CCC and 137 in Neuron (section 4.2).

Isn’t the Sigsheet tool a bridge, like ckb-msig?

  • No. ckb-msig converted between the formats wallets already write, and someone stayed in the middle.
  • With Sigsheet, wallets don’t talk to each other through the tool. Every wallet writes to the same file, and anyone merges the copies.
  • The tool is a signer’s way in, for wallets that don’t read Sigsheet yet. Two libraries, in TypeScript and Rust, let any wallet read it natively, and then its signers don’t need the tool.
  • It’s one week of seven: $300 of the $2,000. The rest pays for the two libraries, the cross-tool demo, specification v0.1 with its tests and documentation, and maintenance.

Does Sigsheet need CCC, ckb-cli or Neuron to change?

  • No. The TypeScript library is its own package on @ckb-ccc/core as published, so any CCC app can use it today. On ccc#646, CCC’s maintainer said CCC currently has no plans to include Sigsheet itself, and welcomed progress updates here on Nervos Talk.
  • ckb-cli’s and Neuron’s maintainers have the spec (#694, #3518), and nothing in v0.1 waits for them. If maintainers later agree to include Sigsheet, ILE Labs will say so in a comment on this thread.

What if ckb-cli and Neuron never include it? Then their users sign with the official ckb-cli and Neuron, through the Sigsheet tool. Every file is the same Sigsheet, checked against the same vectors.

Why not a hosted multisig wallet? A hosted wallet removes the exchange when every member uses it, and its server holds the transactions and signatures. Sigsheet is for groups whose members sign with different tools, on any of the three multisig deployments, with nothing hosted. v0.2’s optional relay automates delivery for those who want it.

Isn’t this the same as tools that check a transaction before signing? Checking the inputs is one part of Sigsheet. The file carries every previous transaction, and each is checked by hash. Sigsheet’s main job is the part one signer can’t do alone: signatures from different tools in one file, kept per signer, merged in any order with the same result, and finalized by anyone.

Is it safe to use for funds?

  • Sigsheet never signs and holds no keys. Each signer signs in their own wallet.
  • A reader takes each lock’s kind from the chain, never from the file.
  • A signature that doesn’t verify for this exact transaction isn’t accepted.
  • Each of the 18 attack vectors says what a reader must do: refuse the file, or drop its signatures.
  • The chain checks every signature again.

Who uses it first? Groups whose members already sign in different tools: payout signers, team treasuries and contract upgraders (section 3.2). v0.1 works on the transactions ckb-cli, CCC apps and Neuron build, not yet on ckb-cli’s deploy files.

item.title: Oracell: Contention-Free Witness Oracle for Nervos CKB (Phase 1 MVP Live on Pudge — Feedback Welcome)
item.dc:creator: RikoKurnia
item.description:
Hi everyone,

I’ve been working on Oracell, a contention-free oracle infrastructure built natively for Nervos CKB’s Cell Model as part of the CKB Builder Track (Week 11–12). Following initial architecture discussions, Phase 1 (MVP) is now live on Pudge Testnet (rikokurnia/oracell on GitHub, live app at oracell [dot] vercel [dot] app), and I’d love to gather technical feedback from the wider CKB community before moving into Phase 2.

The Problem We’re Solving

Traditional push-based oracles map poorly onto CKB’s Extended UTXO (Cell) architecture:

  1. Cell Contention: Updating a single shared price cell destroys its previous OutPoint, causing concurrent DeFi liquidations or swaps referencing that cell in the same block to fail.
  2. Cherry-Picking / Stale Quote Risks: Because CKB-VM scripts execute deterministically without access to global block height or wall-clock time, loose signature windows allow latency arbitrage against older quotes.
  3. Capacity Rent: Requiring every consuming dApp to maintain and mutate its own on-chain price cell increases state rent and cycle overhead.

Phase 1 Architecture & What’s Live

Instead of mutating a shared oracle cell, Oracell delivers signed multi-source market quotes (aggregated from CEX feeds with CKB anchor metadata) directly through the transaction witness:

  • Stateless Witness Verification: @oracell/sdk packs a 184-byte BIP-340 Schnorr proof into WitnessArgs.output_type without consuming any shared oracle cell—allowing parallel transactions in the same block with zero contention.
  • Tip-Header Binding (header_deps): Each quote commits to a recent CKB block hash. The on-chain RISC-V verifier (oracell-verifier) enforces a two-block freshness window relative to supplied header_deps, while the SDK proof runner checks the live RPC tip at submission.
  • Hosted API & SDK: Both ESM and CommonJS clients of @oracell/sdk work out of the box against our hosted /api/oracle/feeds and /api/oracle/quote endpoints without requiring a local server.

Verified Pudge Proof & Benchmarks

  • Code Cell Deployment (Pudge): Tx 0xb2834f4487155d69fa5780a40819196cca1f818a3e62175bb9f2f39a7aeac0b1 (Block 23,135,440, 102,616 bytes RISC-V ELF, data2)
  • Confirmed Consuming Transaction: Tx 0x14beb0d8c0bc0b2a2f1c4aa788c3171284b4c5443074a28059e234cc5bf0ee90 (Block 23,135,450, 5,530,230 RPC cycles)
  • CKB-VM Emulator Contention Benchmark:
    • Shared-cell baseline: 1 / 20 transactions admitted (19 cell contention conflicts)
    • Oracell stateless witness: 100 / 100 transactions verified (0 conflicts, 3,886,926 cycles per verification)

Explicit Phase 1 Boundaries

To be completely transparent about current limitations:

  1. Single Publisher Key: Phase 1 uses a single pinned BIP-340 Schnorr publisher key. Distributed key generation (DKG), threshold Schnorr aggregation (MuSig2 / FROST), and CKB collateral staking/slashing are scoped for Phase 3.
  2. Relative header_deps Freshness: Because CKB-VM cannot read global state or the live network tip, the on-chain two-block window is evaluated relative to the transaction’s supplied header_deps. In production DeFi/L2 flows, this is paired with client/co-signer tip verification at submission time.

Before scoping a follow-up milestone (Phase 2), I would appreciate feedback from CKB developers on three questions:

  1. CellScript Integration: Would a native CellScript helper/module for consuming Oracell’s 184-byte witness proof be useful for teams building CKB-Native DeFi protocols?
  2. Fiber Network & Perun Use Cases: For builders working on Fiber or Perun, is there active demand for discrete Schnorr nonces / DLC adaptor attestations for conditional swaps, hedging, or dispute resolution?
  3. Testnet Early Adopters: Are any teams building on Pudge interested in testing @oracell/sdk in a live dApp (lending, DEX, or hedging) and sharing integration friction points?

Thanks in advance for taking a look—any critique on the verifier design, witness format, or roadmap priorities is very welcome.

item.title: Crowns: a live 3D car race on CKB where the chain is the referee
item.dc:creator: Kaylah
item.description:
Hi everyone I’m Chioma, a builder in the CKBuilders program. I’ve been building Crowns, a real-time 3D car race where players put CKB on the line and the chain decides who won. It’s live on testnet, and I’d love for you to race it and tell me what you think.

Play: https://keepers-relay.vercel.app (testnet)
Code: GitHub - Kaylahray/keepers_relay: Crowns: live 3D car races on Nervos CKB. 2–5 players race 3 laps for a shared pot; each phone signs its own moves, and the chain replays the whole race before paying the winner. Rust rules on CKB-VM and in WebAssembly, Spore trophies, testnet. · GitHub
Build thread: Crowns: a live multiplayer skill game where CKB-VM replays every run · Issue #45 · Nervos-Community-Catalyst/CKBuilder-projects · GitHub

Why I built it

In most online games with money on them, you have to trust the server. It holds the money, it decides who won, and you can’t check either. I wanted a fast, real-time game where nobody has to be trusted: not me, not the server. The chain holds the money and replays the race itself before it pays anyone.

What it is

A race for 2 to 5 players: 3 laps, everyone driving at the same time, with items, boosts and crashes. Races come in two kinds:

  • Entry races: everyone puts in the same entry fee in CKB, and the winner takes the whole pot.
  • Sponsored races: the host puts up the prize and you join free. You only lock a deposit for your seat, and it all comes back after the race.

In the game:

  • 3 tracks: Harbour Loop (the fast one), Switchback Hill (tight hairpins) and Old Town (narrow streets), each with its own scenery.
  • 8 items from pads on the road: Ram, Slick, Jolt, Barricade, Crown Rush, Ward, Patch and Draft. Crashes and hits cost health, and a wrecked car stops for a moment before it rejoins.
  • Phone or computer: on a phone, touch the left or right side of the screen to steer, with buttons for boost and brake. On a computer, use the keyboard.
  • Free practice against two bots on the same rules, with no wallet.
  • Trophies: win a race and claim a trophy, a Spore you own. You can only get one for a race you really won, and the CKB inside it stays yours.
  • Profiles: claim an @username, which is a cell you own on chain. Upload a picture or pick a ready-made look, and it’s minted as a Spore you own and set as your profile picture. Your trophies, wins and crown shards show on your profile and on the leaderboard.
  • Replays: anyone can open a finished race, see each driver’s time, shards and moves, and watch it again in 3D, rebuilt from the moves stored on chain.

How a race works

  1. Host: someone opens a race and picks the track, the number of seats and when it starts (5 to 60 minutes). They either set an entry fee, or sponsor a prize and let players in free.
  2. Join: players take a seat. Each player who joins takes a fifth off the time left.
  3. Start: when the clock reaches zero, everyone is taken into the race at the same moment, with a 10-second countdown.
  4. Payout: when the race ends, the winner is paid automatically. If nobody finishes, everyone gets their money back, and a sponsor gets their prize back.

Your wallet only asks you once, when you join. While you race, your browser signs your moves with a temporary session key, so there are no popups mid-race.

How CKB makes it fair

  • No one holds the money. The host’s CKB sits in a match cell and each player’s in their own seat cell, all locked by the match script, live-match. Not me, not the server.
  • The chain is the referee. The finish transaction carries every car’s moves. live-match spawns the game script with ckb-script-ipc and calls it like a function: judge(record) replays the whole race tick by tick and returns each car’s place. Only then does live-match pay out.
  • Nobody can fake a win. Each player’s moves are signed by their own session key, and the script checks the winner’s signature. The race server (a small relay) passes moves between phones in real time, but it can’t invent them.
  • Money can’t get stuck. If the relay disappears, every entry can go back to its owner after a timeout the chain enforces, with nobody else’s signature.
  • Sponsored races can’t be farmed. Joining one needs a username cell in your wallet, which the chain checks through a cell dep, and the chain refuses one wallet taking two seats in a prize race.
  • One set of rules everywhere. The race rules are one Rust crate with integer maths only, compiled to RISC-V for CKB-VM and to WebAssembly for the browser and the relay, so all three always agree on who won.
  • Anyone can check it. The results page reads the moves from the finish transaction, replays the race in your browser and checks it against who the chain paid.

Status on testnet

  • live-match (type ID): 0xcf2c00c07441a48baeb76284e8edb8d10c6e016865c3eb6b1f87ad3b57a146b7
  • Latest upgrade, sponsored races (22 Nov): 0x4e13e90f…57d4
  • First sponsored race: a 100 CKB prize, and the winner got their deposit back plus the prize. 70,475,122 cycles: 0x8e3bca44…f623
  • A close entry race on 23 Nov: won by 1.5 seconds with 251 signed moves, and the whole race was replayed on chain before paying 200 CKB. 65,322,821 cycles: 0xcef2e225…d515
  • 49 transaction tests in ckb-testtool on the real RISC-V binaries, plus an OffCKB devnet test of seven full races with a real relay and bot drivers.

The cycle counts above are the chain’s own. You can check them yourself: paste either hash into ckb-cycle-tools. It replays the finish in your browser and splits it per script: for the 23 Nov race, live-match and the game it spawns are 63.5M of the 65.3M (97.3%), and the replay matches the node’s total exactly. The worst case (5 cars, full 3 minutes, twistiest track) is about 141M in my tests.

Things I learned on CKB

  • Spawn and IPC make a game a library. live-match doesn’t know anything about racing. It only asks a game script “who won?”. Any game that serves the same trait could use the same match script and its money rules.
  • Same result everywhere needs integer maths. One float anywhere and the phone and the chain would disagree. Fixed ticks and integer maths keep the browser, the relay and CKB-VM in step.
  • Profile the spawned script on its own. In a spawn, the match script is the parent (VM 0) and the game is a child (VM 1), so a plain profile only sees the parent. With ckb-debugger --vm-id 1 and ckb-cycle-tools, which can profile a spawned script on its own, I found that about half of the game’s cycles go to one function that finds the nearest point on the track. That’s where my next cut goes.
  • A cell dep is a free check. The sponsored-race username pass is read as a cell dep, so it costs the player nothing and the cell isn’t spent.
  • Signing live moves needs ordering. I found that key presses sent as separate web requests could reach the relay out of order. The phone then refused to sign a list it didn’t recognise, and a winner could lose the prize. Now each phone has one WebSocket, and every press is numbered.

What it doesn’t do yet

  • One relay. Only my relay runs races today. It can’t cheat, but if it’s down, races wait for the timeout refund.
  • Reload mid-race: a driver who reloads gets back into the race, but can’t sign the moves made before the reload yet.
  • Usernames are checked as free by the app before you claim one. Making that fully on chain is next.
  • Looks: each car is just its seat’s colour. Car skins you own as Spores, richer environments and real car models are next.

What I’d love feedback on

  • How does racing feel on your phone? Is the steering responsive, and is the lag OK?
  • Is anything confusing for someone new to CKB?
  • About half the replay is a nearest-point search on the track. Has anyone made a search like this cheaper in CKB-VM?
  • Each phone signs its moves with a session key, and the chain checks only the winner’s signature before paying. Do you see a gap in that, or a more CKB-native way to do it?

It’s on testnet. Look for the gold Free entry races: you can join those without paying anything. Or grab some testnet CKB from the faucet and host your own, and share the link with friends: it shows a preview card of the race.

Thanks for reading!

item.title: Using the CKBHash Function in CKB Development
item.dc:creator: jm9k
item.description:
CKBHash is a term you might see within the various CKB libraries, and for basic usage it’s abstracted away for you. For more advanced lock design you need to understand what it is and where it is commonly applied. We put together a quick guide to explain how these conventions work.

Using the CKBHash Function in CKB Development

When building smart contracts on CKB you are free to use any cryptographic function that you wish to use. However, many of the system scripts and within the commonly used libraries rely on Blake2b.

In this post we describe some of the specific CKB conventions on how to use it properly with the existing foundations. In most cases, you will rely on libraries that handle all of these details for you. However, advanced smart contract designs might benefit from understanding the specifics of how it is commonly used on CKB.

The CKB Blake2b Standard (ckbhash)

Within the libraries you will find a function called “ckbhash”. This is the a specific configuration of Blake2b:

  • Algorithm: blake2b-256 (outputs 32 bytes).
  • Personalization: “ckb-default-hash”.
  • Common Variant: blake160 (blake2b-256 truncated to first 20 bytes (160 bits)).

Blake2b-256 is always used for the ckbhash function. However, you will see some places that reference “blake160”. This is still blake2b-256, but the hash hash been truncated to the first 20 byptes (160 bits).

The ckbhash function automatically applies the “ckb-default-hash” personalization, so you never need to manually configure the blake2b parameters when using library functions.

Common Uses in CKB

The ckbhash function is used throughout CKB for:

  1. Secp256k1 Lock Arg (Blake160) - The Secp256k1 lock requires a ckbhash of the public key truncated to the first 20 bytes.
  2. Script Hash Calculation - Hashing serialized script structures for identification.
  3. Transaction Hashing - Creating transaction identifiers (excluding witnesses).
  4. Transaction Witness Hash - Hashing the complete serialized transaction including witnesses for block headers.
  5. Cell Data Hashing - Generating data hashes for type scripts and cell references.
  6. Signing Message Construction - Creating the message to sign by hashing tx hash plus witness data.

1. Public Key to Secp256k1 Lock Arg (Blake160)

Converts an secp256k1 public key into the required arg for the commonly used secp256k1_blake160_sighash_all lock, which is used in most wallets.

import { SignerCkbPrivateKey, ccc } from "@ckb-ccc/core";

const signer = new SignerCkbPrivateKey(new ccc.ClientPublicTestnet(), privateKey);
const lockArg = (await signer.getAddressObjSecp256k1()).script.args;  // Internally: ckbhash(publicKey).slice(0, 20)

2. Script Hash Calculation

Generates a unique identifier for any script by hashing its serialized structure, which is used for script identification and locating cells.

import { Script } from "@ckb-ccc/core";

const script = new Script(
	"0x9bd7e06f3ecf4be0f2fcd2188b23f1b9fcc88e5d4b65a8637b17723bbda3cce8",	// codeHash
	"type",																	// hashType
	"0xb39bbc0b3673c7d36450bc14cfcdad2d559c6c64"							// args
);

const scriptHash = script.hash();  // Internally: ckbhash(molecule_encode(script))

3. Transaction Hashing

Creates a unique identifier for transactions by hashing the raw transaction data, which excludes witnesses and is used for transaction references.

import { Transaction } from "@ckb-ccc/core";

const tx = new Transaction(/* ... */);
const txHash = tx.hash();  // Internally: ckbhash(molecule_encode(raw_transaction))

4. Transaction Witness Hash

Computes the complete transaction hash including all witness data, which is used in block headers for the witness merkle tree.

import { Transaction } from "@ckb-ccc/core";

const tx = new Transaction(/* ... */);
const witnessHash = tx.hashFull();  // Internally: ckbhash(molecule_encode(full_transaction))

5. Cell Data Hashing

Generates a hash of cell data content, which is used by type scripts for data integrity verification and locating cells.

import { HasherCkb } from "@ckb-ccc/core";

const hasher = new HasherCkb();
hasher.update(cellData);
const dataHash = hasher.digest();  // Internally: ckbhash(cellData)

6. Signing Message Construction

Builds the final message to be signed by combining transaction hash with witness data, which ensures signatures cover the complete transaction context.

import { Signer } from "@ckb-ccc/core";

const signature = await signer.signTransaction(tx);  // Internally: sign(ckbhash(txHash + witnessData))

Complete Example with CCC

This example demonstrates the complete workflow from private key to script hash, showing how ckbhash is used at multiple stages: first to generate the blake160 lock arg from a public key, then to create a unique script identifier.

import { Script, SignerCkbPrivateKey, ccc } from "@ckb-ccc/core";

// Create signer from private key
const client = new ccc.ClientPublicTestnet();
const signer = new SignerCkbPrivateKey(client, "0xd00c06bfd800d27397002dca6fb0993d5ba6399b4238b2f29ee9deb97593d2bc");

// Get blake160 lock arg
const lockArg = (await signer.getAddressObjSecp256k1()).script.args;

// Create lock script
const lockScript = new Script(
	"0x9bd7e06f3ecf4be0f2fcd2188b23f1b9fcc88e5d4b65a8637b17723bbda3cce8",  // mainnet secp256k1
	"type",
	lockArg
);

// Get script hash
const scriptHash = lockScript.hash();

Further Reading

  • How to Sign a Transaction - Detailed explanation of transaction signing process.
  • CCC Documentation - Official CCC usage guide.
  • CKB System Scripts Repository - Source code for all CKB system scripts.
  • CKB RFCs - Transaction Structure (RFC 0022) - Defines the official ckbhash function specification.
  • CKB RFCs - Genesis Script List (RFC 0024) - Lists all system scripts including secp256k1_blake160_sighash_all.

item.title: Understanding CKB Lock Value Relationships
item.dc:creator: jm9k
item.description:
When you work with the CKB Cell Model, there are a lot of different lock values and the terminology can be confusing at first. Even for a seasoned developer, how all these values fit together is often overlooked. This is why we are sharing this guide to explain it in simple terms.

Understanding CKB Lock Value Relationships

In CKB smart contract development, it is important to understand how different lock-related values connect to each other. These values form a chain of cryptographic relationships that are used throughout smart contract development for purposes such as ownership verification, address generation, and cross-referencing between different scripts.

The Value Derivation Chain

Here’s how all lock-related values connect in CKB at a high level:

Understanding Each Value

Below we will explain each of the values and their relationships with each other in more detail. On CKB you can use any cryptographic algorithm you want, but most wallets rely on secp256k1 because that is what is used for the fallback lock secp256k1-blake160-sighash-all. Our descriptions and examples will all assume this lock.

Private Key (32 bytes)

The chain starts with a secret private key that is never shared but used to prove ownership. This is your fundamental credential for controlling CKB cells and assets.

// Private keys are represented as hex strings in CCC.
const privateKey = "0xd00c06bfd800d27397002dca6fb0993d5ba6399b4238b2f29ee9deb97593d2bc";

Why it matters: Your private key is the root of all ownership verification in CKB. During transaction validation, you use this key to create digital signatures that prove you control specific cells without revealing the key itself.

Further Learning:

  • Public Key Cryptography (YouTube Video)

Public Key (33 bytes)

The public key is derived from the private key using secp256k1 elliptic curve cryptography. This is the shareable counterpart to your private key that enables others to verify your signatures.

import {SignerCkbPrivateKey, ccc} from "@ckb-ccc/core";

// Initialize CCC client (testnet example).
const client = new ccc.ClientPublicTestnet();

// Create a signer from the private key.
const signer = new SignerCkbPrivateKey(client, privateKey);
const publicKey = signer.publicKey;
// Example: 0x03fe6c6d09d1a0f70255cddf25c5ed57d41b5c08822ae710dc10f8c88290e0acdf (33 bytes).

// Or derive manually using secp256k1.
// const secp256k1 = require('secp256k1');
// const publicKey = "0x" + Buffer.from(secp256k1.publicKeyCreate(Buffer.from(privateKey.slice(2), 'hex'), true)).toString('hex');

Why it matters: Your public key enables signature verification without exposing your private key. It’s also the starting point for generating your unique account identifier (lock arg) that distinguishes your cells from all other users.

Further Learning:

  • Public Key Cryptography (YouTube Video)

Lock Arg (20 bytes)

The lock arg is generated by applying ckbhash to the public key and taking the first 20 bytes (blake160). This is the same length as both Bitcoin and Ethereum.

import {hashCkb, ccc} from "@ckb-ccc/core";

// Derive from public key to show the transformation.
const lockArg = hashCkb(publicKey).slice(0, 42);
// Example: "0xc8328aabcd9b9e8e64fbc566c4385c3bdeb219d7" (20 bytes).

// Or get it from an address object.
// const addressObj = await signer.getAddressObjSecp256k1();
// const lockArg = addressObj.script.args;

Why it matters: This value uniquely identifies your “account” when placed in the args field of the secp256k1-blake160-sighash-all lock script. The args value is how the code knows who owns the cell. It serves as an identifier for the basis of authentication, and also a label on cells that can be searched for when building transactions.

Further Learning:

  • Using the CKBHash Function in CKB Development
  • secp256k1_blake160_sighash_all Script Implementation

Lock Script (Structure)

The complete script structure that defines cell ownership. This identifies the script code that is executed with your unique identifier to create a lock that is only accessible with your private key.

import {Script, ccc} from "@ckb-ccc/core";

// Create a lock script using CCC.
const lockScript = ccc.Script.from({
	codeHash: "0x9bd7e06f3ecf4be0f2fcd2188b23f1b9fcc88e5d4b65a8637b17723bbda3cce8",
	hashType: "type",
	args: "0xc8328aabcd9b9e8e64fbc566c4385c3bdeb219d7"
});

// Or get it from an address object.
// const addressObj = await signer.getAddressObjSecp256k1();
// const lockScript = addressObj.script;

Key components:

  • codeHash: The hash that identifies the script code to execute.
  • hashType: Used to indicate how to interpret the code hash.
  • args: Your unique identifier (the lock arg derived from your public key).

Why it matters: A lock script is a structure that defines ownership rules for cells. It specifies script code (smart contract) that will execute to validate ownership and arguments provided to the code (lock arg) that determine who can access it.

Further Learning:

  • Introduction to CKB Script Programming
  • Build a Simple Lock Script

Lock Hash (32 bytes)

A unique identifier for the complete lock script structure, calculated by hashing the script structure after being serialized with molecule.

import {hashCkb, ccc} from "@ckb-ccc/core";

// Manual calculation to show the transformation.
const lockHash = hashCkb(lockScript.toBytes());
// Example: "0x32e555f3ff8e135cece1351a6a2971518392c1e30375c1e006ad0ce8eac07947".

// Or use the built-in method (more common).
// const lockHash = lockScript.hash();
// This performs: hashCkb(molecule_encode(lockScript)).

Why it matters: A lock script is a structure comprised of a code hash, hash type, and lock args. This complete component structure is what determines ownership of cells, but it’s not easily referenced since it is three long fields. By serializing and hashing the lock script into a lock hash we end up with a space-efficient identifier that can be easily referenced by smart contracts.

Further Learning:

  • Serialization and Molecule in CKB
  • Molecule Serialization Specification
  • Molecule Tools Documentation
  • Script Hash Calculation in CKB

Address (Human-Readable)

The single line representation of your lock script that encodes all the data about the lock script structure in a human-readable format that’s easy to share and has checksum validation to prevent mistakes.

import {ccc} from "@ckb-ccc/core";

// Create address from lock script to show the transformation.
const address = ccc.Address.fromScript(lockScript, client).toString();
// Example: "ckt1qzda0cr08m85hc8jlnfp3zer7xulejywt49kt2rr0vthywaa50xwsqwgx292hnvmn68xf779vmzrshpmm6epn4c0cgwga".

// Or get it directly from the signer (more common).
// const address = (await signer.getAddressObjSecp256k1()).toString();

Why it matters: Addresses provide a standardized way to share the complete lock script structure in a way that is human-readable and also reversible. A lock hash is similar in that it provides a more concise way to reference a lock script, but since it uses one-way hashing the full lock script structure cannot be extracted. When transferring funds to someone the full lock script is needed, which is why addresses must be used instead of lock hashes.

Further Learning:

  • CKB Address Technical Explanation
  • CKB RFC 0021: CKB Address Format

Acquiring Values with CCC

Here’s how to obtain each lock-related value using CCC as the library was designed to be used. Rather than manually calculating each transformation, CCC provides high-level methods that handle the derivation chain internally:

import {SignerCkbPrivateKey, Script, ccc} from "@ckb-ccc/core";

// Initialize CCC client.
const client = new ccc.ClientPublicTestnet(); // Use ClientPublicMainnet() for mainnet.

// 1. Start with a private key.
const privateKey = "0xd00c06bfd800d27397002dca6fb0993d5ba6399b4238b2f29ee9deb97593d2bc";

// Create signer from private key.
const signer = new SignerCkbPrivateKey(client, privateKey);

// 2. Get public key from signer.
const publicKey = signer.publicKey;

// Get complete address object (contains all derived values).
const addressObj = await signer.getAddressObjSecp256k1();

// 3. Extract lock arg from address object.
const lockArg = addressObj.script.args;

// 4. Extract lock script from address object.
const lockScript = addressObj.script;

// 5. Calculate lock hash from lock script.
const lockHash = lockScript.hash();

// 6. Get human-readable address.
const address = addressObj.toString();

console.log("Lock Value Chain:");
console.log(`1. Private Key: ${privateKey}`);
console.log(`2. Public Key: ${publicKey}`);
console.log(`3. Lock Arg: ${lockArg}`);
console.log(`4. Lock Script:`, lockScript);
console.log(`5. Lock Hash: ${lockHash}`);
console.log(`6. Address: ${address}`);

For a complete working example with both CCC and Lumos implementations, see the Lock Value Relationships Demo (GitHub).

Further Learning

Additional resources and learning materials are available for those interested in deepening their understanding of CKB development.

  • Nervos Developer Documentation
  • Nervos University
  • Lock Value Relationships Demo (GitHub)

item.title: Design Patterns: UTXO Transfers Using the Cell Model
item.dc:creator: jm9k
item.description:
How to transfer assets with the Cell Model is a surprisingly complex subject because of the state rent requirements. We wanted to share a guide on seven patterns (both current and future) that developers should understand.

Design Patterns: UTXO Transfers Using the Cell Model

This document explores different patterns for transferring digital assets between two parties using the Nervos CKB Cell Model. While focused on the CKB blockchain, these patterns may also apply to other UTXO blockchains that implement state rent.

State rent is essential because it ensures sustainable network economics and prevents out of control cost spirals. However, it introduces unique challenges that require innovative design patterns to maintain usability.

Some of the transfer patterns mentioned in this document are tied directly to specific asset protocols. This document aims to focus specifically on the transfer patterns introduced, not the details of the asset protocols themselves.

Challenges of State Rent

State rent presents unique obstacles for UTXO-based token transfers that don’t exist in traditional blockchain models. Understanding these challenges is essential for designing effective transfer patterns.

CKB implements state rent through a simple economic model: 1 CKB token equals 1 byte of permanent on-chain storage capacity. When you create a cell containing smart contracts, assets such as tokens and NFTs, or any other data, the cell’s capacity must cover the storage cost of all these components. This capacity remains locked the entire time the asset exists on-chain. When the assets are destroyed and the cell is consumed, the locked CKB is returned.

The amount of CKB that must be locked depends on the amount of required on-chain data, which can vary from asset to asset. For the most basic asset, the CKB native token, the cost is 61 CKB. For an SUDT token, the cost is 142 CKB. For assets such as NFTs, the cost varies but is usually in the 150-200 CKB range. For fully on-chain DOBs, the cost can easily exceed thousands of CKB.

The challenge is that when you send an asset to someone else, a cell must be created to hold it. This introduces additional costs to the sender if they pay the state rent for the receiver. However, there are multiple patterns to mitigate this depending on the situation.

Cell Model Asset Transfer Design Patterns

Several patterns can be used to address state rent costs for asset transfers. Each pattern balances simplicity, cost distribution, and trust requirements differently.

In the diagrams below, each box is a cell that holds assets and CKB capacity. A blue border marks a cell that is new or changed in that step. A yellow box is a cell with special rules, such as an ACP cell. Transaction fees are left out for simplicity.

Sender Pays State Rent Pattern

The sender covers all state rent costs for the receiver’s new cell. The asset transfer creates a cell owned by the receiver with capacity paid entirely by the sender.

Pros:

  • Most simple and compatible method to implement.
  • No CKB requirements for receiver.
  • Single step process.

Cons:

  • Sender must pay extra CKB for the receiver’s cell.
  • Scales poorly as CKB price increases.
  • Costs create high barriers for frequent transfers.

Send and Refund Pattern

The sender pays state rent initially, then the receiver refunds the CKB capacity back to the sender. This requires trust on the part of the sender, and the receiver must actively participate after receiving the asset.

Pros:

  • Sender does not pay the CKB for the receiver’s cell.
  • Conceptually simple process that is easy to implement.

Cons:

  • Receiver must have CKB to pay the refund.
  • Receiver must be trusted to send back the CKB.
  • Requires automated bots for receiving applications.
  • No automated solutions exist for user to user transfers.

Anyone-Can-Pay (ACP) Pattern

The receiver creates a special cell which unlocks for any user when it detects that it is receiving additional assets, but remains securely locked in other scenarios. This is similar to a mail drop box, where anyone can make a deposit but it’s not possible to take anything back out.

The receiver must create an ACP cell ahead of time to hold the specific asset they want to receive. This only needs to be done once per asset, and then it can receive indefinitely.

Pros:

  • Sender does not pay the CKB for the receiver’s cell (after refund).
  • Mature and tested pattern and implementation.
  • No trust requirements.

Cons:

  • Receiver must have CKB to create the ACP cell.
  • ACP cells must be pre-deployed by receivers for each asset.
  • Limited wallet and tooling support.
  • More complex smart contract logic.

Resources:

  • Anyone-Can-Pay Lock Script RFC - Official specification for ACP lock script.
  • Anyone-Can-Pay Repository - Current implementation and documentation.
  • OmniLock Repository - Advanced lock script that also supports anyone-can-pay functionality.

Cheque Cell Pattern

Implements a mechanism similar to a bank cheque where the sender creates a special cell that can be “cashed” by the receiver. The receiver must provide their own CKB capacity to claim the asset, and the CKB used for the cheque cell is returned to the sender. If the cheque remains unclaimed after 6 epochs, the sender can withdraw the assets and reclaim the capacity.

Pros:

  • Sender does not pay the CKB for the receiver’s cell.
  • Does not require the receiver to pre-deploy asset receiver cells.
  • No trust requirements.

Cons:

  • Receiver must have CKB to claim assets to a cell they own.
  • Unclaimed assets require the sender to undergo another step to recover.
  • Very limited wallet and tooling support.
  • More complex smart contract logic.

Resources:

  • Cheque Lock RFC - Official RFC specification for cheque lock, including example transactions.
  • Cheque Lock Script - Official cheque script implementation and documentation.

CoTA (Compact Token Aggregator) Pattern

CoTA is an NFT protocol which uses Sparse Merkle Trees (SMT) to manage large amounts of data off-chain while maintaining security guarantees on-chain. CoTA can be thought of as a layer 1.5 protocol that operates internally using the account-model, storing both data and ownership information in a distributed cell structure on top of UTXOs.

Each user creates a single permanent CoTA cell that becomes part of the distributed asset registry. Inside of each CoTA cell is a single SMT root hash consisting of exactly 32 bytes that provide provable information about the assets contained within the cell. The amount of data remains the same in a CoTA cell regardless of how many NFTs or how much data is associated with the user. An unlimited amount of NFTs can be created and held without increasing state rent costs.

CoTA builds on its distributed cell structure to add an innovative transfer mechanism that eliminate the immediate onboarding costs for new users to receive assets. CoTA assets operate on layer 1.5, which uses internal ownership tracking that is separate from the cell model. When assets are transferred on CoTA, they are marked for recipients without leaving the sender’s cell. This means that CoTA NFTs effectively bypass the state rent requirements, allowing NFTs to be minted for near-zero cost and can be sent to new users who hold no CKB. The caveat being that the receiver cannot transfer an NFT again until they complete the one-time CoTA cell registration process and complete the claim process which moves the NFT from the original sender’s CoTA cell to their own CoTA cell.

The CoTA transfer process involves four distinct stages:

Stage Sender Receiver Transfer Capability Notes
Initial Owns NFT No NFT Transferable The NFT is in the sender’s cell.
After Transfer No NFT Owns Unclaimed NFT Not Transferable Ownership is marked, and the NFT stays in the sender’s cell.
After Registration No NFT Owns Unclaimed NFT Not Transferable The receiver creates a CoTA cell to claim with. This step is optional.
After Claim No NFT Owns Claimed NFT Transferable The NFT is now in the receiver’s cell. This step is optional.

The registration process has a one-time fee of 150CKB, which is non-refundable since the cell that is created effectively becomes part of CoTA’s distributed cell structure. Registration is required to claim an NFT that has been marked for transfer, but it is not a requirement. Recipients will see unclaimed NFTs in their wallets just like normal NFTs, but they must register and claim if they want to send the NFT to someone else.

Pros:

  • Sender does not pay the CKB for the receiver’s CoTA cell.
  • Does not require the receiver to pre-deploy asset receiver cells.
  • Zero state rent cost for unclaimed transfers; claiming is not strictly required.
  • No trust requirements.

Cons:

  • Receiver must have CKB to register a CoTA cell before claiming.
  • CoTA’s layer 1.5 protocol has some incompatibilities with other protocols.
  • Requires an off-chain aggregator service for interpreting data.
  • Limited wallet and tooling support.
  • Transactions are more complex and must be generated using the CoTA SDK in conjunction with an aggregator.

Resources:

  • CoTA Protocol Overview - Official protocol documentation.
  • CoTA SDK JavaScript - JavaScript SDK for CoTA integration.
  • CoTA SDK Examples - Usage examples and integration guides.

Public Relay Cells Pattern (ACP Enhancement; Experimental)

Public relay cells are an optional enhancement to the Anyone-Can-Pay pattern that address the concurrency limitations by introducing public storage cells that act as temporary holding areas for token transfers. This pattern solves the collision problem where multiple simultaneous transfers to the same ACP cell would fail due to the deterministic nature of transfers on CKB.

In addition to increasing throughput to a single address by allowing parallel deposits, relay cells can serve as temporary holding areas for new users who haven’t yet deployed their own ACP cells. This allows new users to receive tokens without any upfront CKB requirement, dramatically lowering the barrier to entry into the ecosystem.

The relay cells are serviced by a decentralized network of fulfillment bots that monitor deposits and deliver tokens to their final destinations. These bots compete to process transfers, earning small fees for providing this collection and delivery service. This creates a permissionless marketplace where anyone can operate a fulfillment bot, ensuring system resilience without single points of failure while creating earning opportunities for operators providing fulfillment services.

Pros:

  • Sender does not pay the CKB for the receiver’s cell.
  • Does not require the receiver to pre-deploy asset receiver cells (ACP cells).
  • No trust requirements.

Cons:

  • Receiver must eventually have CKB to claim assets to a cell they own.
  • Unclaimed assets may be returned or forfeited.
  • Emerging incomplete standard with no implementation.

Challenges:
As this standard is still a work in progress, several challenges remain to be addressed. One concern is the potential for relay cell clogging if tokens remain unclaimed for extended periods. Proposed solutions include implementing asset forfeiture mechanisms after certain timeframes, which would incentivize timely claiming while preventing permanent blockage of relay resources.

Resources:

  • Public Relay Cells Discussion - Original proposal and community discussion on Nervos Talk.

Harbor Pattern (Fractal Standard; Experimental)

Harbor is a pattern within the Fractal token standard which is currently in early development stages. The Fractal standard takes inspiration from CoTA, using Sparse Merkle Trees (SMT) to manage asset data off-chain while maintaining security guarantees on-chain. However, Fractal utilizes the Cell Model for ownership designation instead of a layer 1.5 account model structure. Harbors have similarities to public relay cells in being publicly available areas for asset storage, but Harbors can be used both as temporary storage and permanent storage.

A Fractal cell contains a single SMT root hash consisting of exactly 32 bytes, similar to a CoTA cell. The amount of data always remains the same regardless of how many assets are associated with the user, allowing for an unlimited amount of assets to be held without increasing state rent costs. A Fractal cell uses normal locks and allows the owner to control all assets within the cell.

A Harbor cell is a special kind of Fractal cell, which is created by anyone for public use. Anyone can store a Fractal asset in any Harbor by paying a small “parking fee” to the operator. Multiple Harbors can be created by anyone to create a competitive marketplace that keeps fees reasonable while providing parallelism for concurrent transfers. Should an operator wish to close their Harbor to recoup the CKB being used for state rent, they are free to do so at any time. However, if there are any Fractal assets stored within the harbor they are trying to close, they must migrate them to another open harbor and pay the parking fee for each asset.

Harbor cells can serve as holding areas for new users who haven’t yet acquired any CKB to create their own Fractal cell, allowing them to bypass the state rent requirements. Since Fractal cells can hold any number of assets, they never will experience a “clogging” scenario that could happen with a public relay cell. For this reason, a Fractal cell is suitable for permanent storage. However, some smart contracts may not be able to operate normally with assets in a Harbor, and may still require withdrawal to a normal Fractal cell.

Note: The Fractal standard and Harbor pattern are in very early development and specifications may change significantly.

The Harbor transfer process involves up to four distinct stages:

Stage Sender Receiver Transfer Capability Notes
Initial Owns Assets No Assets Transferable The assets are in the sender’s cell or a Harbor cell.
After Transfer No Assets Owns Assets in Harbor Transferable Ownership is marked, and the assets move to a Harbor cell.
After Registration No Assets Owns Assets in Harbor Transferable The receiver creates a Fractal cell to claim with. This step is optional.
After Claim No Assets Owns Assets Transferable The assets move to the receiver’s cell. This step is optional.

The registration process requires 150CKB to create a Fractal cell, which is refundable if the cell is later destroyed. Registration is required to claim assets that have been stored in a Harbor, but it is not strictly necessary for ownership. Recipients use Harbor-stored assets as if they were holding them directly and can transfer them to other users as needed.

The following diagram illustrates how these stages work in practice with specific CKB capacity movements:

Pros:

  • Sender does not pay the CKB for the receiver’s cell.
  • Does not require the receiver to pre-deploy asset receiver cells.
  • No trust requirements.

Cons:

  • Receiver must eventually have CKB to claim assets to a cell they own.
  • Requires an off-chain aggregator service for interpreting data.
  • Transactions are more complex and must be generated using the Fractal SDK in conjunction with an aggregator.
  • Emerging incomplete standard with no implementation.

Closing

The Cell Model’s state rent requirement creates unique challenges for asset transfers that have sparked innovative design patterns that offer different trade-offs between simplicity, cost, trust, and user experience.

This document explores seven distinct transfer patterns for addressing state rent challenges in UTXO-based asset transfers:

  1. Sender Pays State Rent - The most straightforward approach where senders cover all capacity costs for receivers’ new cells. While simple to implement and requiring no CKB from receivers, it scales poorly as CKB prices increase and creates barriers for frequent transfers.

  2. Send and Refund - A trust-based pattern where senders initially pay state rent, then receivers refund the capacity. Conceptually simple but requires active receiver participation and trust, with limited automated solutions for user-to-user transfers.

  3. Anyone-Can-Pay (ACP) - A mature, trustless solution using special cells that unlock when receiving assets. Requires receivers to pre-deploy cells for each asset type and has concurrency limitations, but offers proven reliability for users.

  4. Cheque Cell - Implements a bank cheque-like mechanism where senders create claimable cells with automatic withdrawal after timeout. Provides trustless transfers without pre-deployment requirements but adds complexity for managing unclaimed assets.

  5. CoTA (Compact Token Aggregator) - An innovative layer 1.5 protocol using Sparse Merkle Trees for off-chain data management. Virtually eliminates state rent for unclaimed transfers and allows near zero-cost minting, but requires off-chain aggregator infrastructure and has protocol incompatibilities.

  6. Public Relay Cells (Experimental) - An ACP enhancement using intermediate public storage cells to address concurrency limitations. Enables parallel deposits and serves new users without upfront CKB requirements, but relies on decentralized fulfillment bots and remains in experimental stages.

  7. Harbor (Fractal Standard; Experimental) - An emerging pattern within the Fractal token standard that combines the use of Sparse Merkle Trees for off-chain data management with decentralized public cells for asset storage. Allows for near zero-cost minting and eliminates state rent for newly onboarded users. However, the standard is in very early development with no current implementation.

Which Pattern to Use?

For Simple Applications:

  • Use “Sender Pays State Rent” for low-volume transfers where simplicity matters most.
  • Consider “Send and Refund” for applications which inherently require trust and the pattern offers few drawbacks.

For Production Applications:

  • Choose “Anyone-Can-Pay” for mature applications where deposits are made to an application where pre-deploying ACP cells is possible.
  • Select “Cheque Cell” when receivers cannot pre-deploy cells but trustless transfers are essential.
  • Consider “CoTA” for NFT applications where low-cost NFTs and unclaimed transfers provide significant user experience benefits.

For Future Applications:

  • Evaluate “Public Relay Cells” as a solution to scale ACP’s concurrency limitations.
  • Monitor “Harbor” development for future ultra-low-cost asset solutions.
