item.title: CKBA Presents: Question Time with Xiaomao and Noir CKB
item.dc:creator: JackyLHH
item.description:
Noir CKB is a developer toolchain that connects the Noir programming language (for writing zero-knowledge proofs) with the Nervos CKB blockchain.

In simple terms:

Imagine you want to keep a secret number (like a private score or balance) stored on a blockchain, where only you should be able to update it, without ever revealing the number itself.

Noir CKB is an experimental way to write private logic in the relatively friendly Noir language, and safely enforce it on CKB. The Private Tally is the current live demo, you can try on testnet if you want to experiment.

  • Noir is a programming language made for zero-knowledge (ZK) proofs. ZK proofs let you prove “I followed the rules correctly” (e.g., “I added 5 to my secret number”) without showing the secret. Noir has a clean, Rust-like syntax, so it’s more approachable than older ZK languages. Noir was created by Aztec Network.
  • CKB (Common Knowledge Base) is the Layer 1 blockchain of the Nervos Network. It is Bitcoin-inspired (Proof-of-Work, UTXO-style) but flexible and highly programmable. Data lives in “cells,” and small programs called scripts decide how those cells can be updated. Scripts run in CKB-VM (a RISC-V virtual machine).

Noir CKB lets you:

  • Write the rule in Noir (e.g. “new secret = old secret + amount I add”).
  • Generate a ZK proof on your own computer.
  • Submit a transaction on CKB. A Type Script on-chain verifies the proof and checks that the proof is specifically about this cell and this exact state change (right network, right old commitment, right new commitment, etc.).

The key idea of the project is:

“A proof that verifies is not the same as a proof that authorizes this cell transition.”

Xiaomao.

A mathematically perfect proof could still be about the wrong cell or update. Noir CKB binds the proof tightly to the actual transaction so it can’t be reused incorrectly.

The Private Tally is a cell that holds a hidden number.

  • Only the person with the secret key can add to it.
  • Every update is authorized by a zero-knowledge proof generated on their machine.
  • The cell stores only a commitment (a fingerprint of the number + fresh randomness), so the real value stays private.
  • You can add any amount, including 0.
  • There is no normal signature lock; the proof itself is the authority.

On-chain the updates look the same whether you added something or nothing. What stays private is the actual value and the amounts added. Transaction metadata (existence of the tally, timing, who paid fees) is still visible.

It is research / experimental software (pre-audit, testnet only). Not for production or mainnet use yet.

Below is a set of questions targeting the core design trade-offs (binding correctness, performance, trust, tooling, and privacy limits) rather than surface-level features.

We want to pick Xiaomao’s brain on Noir CKB so here it goes:

Hello hello Xiaomao, how’s things? Let’s start with a personal statement, shall we? Who are you, and what is your background?

“My name is Xiaomao, and I’m a ZK and privacy engineer.”

“Most of my work sits in the zero-knowledge and privacy space, what pulls me in is the idea that you can prove something is true without revealing the data behind it. I think privacy is one of the most important problems in this industry. As more of our lives move on-chain, everything being public by default stops being acceptable, and I want to build the tooling that lets people keep private what should stay private, while still proving they followed the rules.”

“For about a year, I worked with Base as a developer in East Africa, where I helped developers get started, ran workshops, and supported the local builder community. These days my focus has gone deeper into the ZK and cryptography side, and I’m building on CKB. If I had to put my focus in one line, it’s privacy, and the practical side of it: bridging the gap between what protocols can do and what builders can actually ship. A lot of powerful cryptography never reaches developers because the distance between the research and a working build is too wide, and closing that gap is the work I care about most.”

“Outside of engineering, community is a big part of what I do. I co-founded LedgerLady, a women-led developer community that trains and equips women to become strong Web3 developers, and we run cohorts and university workshops across East Africa. I’m also an open-source enthusiast and contributor, so a lot of what I build and learn happens in the open.”

Wonderful, I can see you’ve been busy. How did you find out about CKBuilders and what is it like working around other CKBuilders? What interests you about CKB?

“I found CKB through a friend, to be honest. We were just chatting and he told me about a protocol called CKB, which had a builders program, and they asked if I wanted to join. I said sure, and he referred me to Neon, who leads CKBuilders. After talking with Neon I was onboarded, and that’s really when I started learning what CKB is. I hadn’t come across it on my own before that.”

“It’s been a really good experience. Beyond learning CKB itself, the part I didn’t expect to enjoy so much is watching other builders grow and seeing the range of things people are shipping in the CKB space. One thing I found fascinating is that most of us coming in as new CKB devs, came from somewhere else first. Some came from Ethereum, some from Polkadot, some from Bitcoin. A lot of people wrote about that transition, coming from Ethereum, or from Polkadot, and I wrote one too. Watching people make that shift and document it is genuinely beautiful to see.”

“I’ve learned a lot from people in the community, and the thing I appreciate most is that everyone is rooting for each other. There are channels for technical discussion and for reviews, where people actually give you feedback on your work. Something I’ve realized is that it’s not easy to get someone to sit down, use your product, and tell you what they think. So when another builder takes their time to test what you built and give you a real review, that means a lot, and that kind of support is one of the best things about the community.”

“The cell model, and specifically what it does to the way you think about programs. Coming in, I expected smart contracts on CKB to work more or less the way they do on Ethereum. What CKB taught me instead was to think in verifiers. A type script isn’t a function you call to mutate storage. It looks at the old state, the new state, and the evidence, and decides whether that transition is allowed. So instead of thinking in accounts, balances, and function calls, I started thinking in state transitions that have to be verified rather than executed. That shift connected directly to how I already think. While I was learning CKB, I kept coming back to ZK in my head. The verifier mindset made it easy to plug the ZK knowledge I already had straight into CKB, and that’s actually one of the reasons I’m building what I’m building now.
The cell model and ZK proofs fit together more naturally than I expected. Putting a zero knowledge proof inside a type script stops feeling exotic once you see that the script is already a verifier, and the proof is just one more thing it checks before it accepts a transition.”

What advice would you give to anyone looking to build on CKB, and what AI tools would you advise to help anyone on their journey to build on the cell model?

“If you’re a beginner, learn the cell model from first principles before you write anything. If you’re coming from another ecosystem, the important thing is to separate what you already know from how CKB actually works, because they aren’t the same. The cell model is the fundamental thing to understand. Get clear on what a cell is, what capacity means, the difference between lock and type scripts, and what a transaction really is, which is a proposed state transition rather than a function call. Once those are solid, everything else builds on top of them.”

“On AI, I lean on it hard, but as a research and review partner, not as an autopilot. I won’t name specific tools, because I don’t want to push anyone toward one in particular, but in general some models are stronger for research and reasoning through a design, and others are better for coding. I use them to move faster and to pressure test my ideas, and I check everything myself, especially anything new or anything that touches correctness or security.”

Regarding binding and replay protection: the type script rebuilds the public statement from the live transaction before verifying the Groth16 proof.

How do you guarantee that this reconstruction is complete and cannot be gamed by clever transaction construction?

Have you formalized the binding predicate, and what is the strongest attacker model you’ve tested against?

“Honestly, I haven’t formally verified the binding predicate, and I wouldn’t claim it’s provably complete. What I’ve done is make it explicit, and then attack it hard.”

“The type script rebuilds a context digest from the live transaction. That includes the network domain, the consumed cell’s outpoint, the old and new commitments, the successor lock, the capacity, and the action. It hashes that and feeds it in as part of the proof’s public inputs, so the proof only verifies if the statement it was made for matches the transaction it’s actually sitting in. A valid proof for one cell, one network, or one transition won’t be verified anywhere else.”

“The strongest attacker model I’ve tested is someone who can build arbitrary transactions and replay proofs they’ve observed. The Private Tally’s type script runs against a 49-case adversarial CKB-VM matrix plus mutation tests, and the cases that matter here are exactly the kind you’d worry about: multiple same-type inputs in a group, a proof replayed on a different outpoint, a proof replayed on a different tally cell, a capacity change on update, a proof made for a different network, and a creation proof reused as an update. All of them are rejected. The mutation tests then remove each check one at a time and confirm that the attack the check exists to stop gets through without it, so I know each check is doing real work and not just sitting there.”

“The honest limits: the binding is per state transition, not per whole transaction. Fee inputs and change are deliberately left open, which means a third party can pay the fee or relay the exact transition the key holder authorized. They can’t change what it does, but that’s a real property people should know about. And testing against a set of adversarial transactions is not the same as proving no adversarial transaction exists. It’s pre-audit software. Part of why I’m building the generator, which is the next question, is to make the binding predicate come from a small, reviewable spec instead of hand-written script logic, so that the thing you’d formally verify is small and explicit.”

There are CKB-VM cycle costs and practical limits, right?

Groth16 verification is currently landing in the ~100–120 million cycle range on CKB-VM.

What is the realistic upper bound on circuit size / public inputs before a proof becomes uneconomical or hits the cycle limit, and have you profiled the dominant costs (pairing, multi-scalar multiplication, Molecule decoding)?

Are there planned optimizations (precompiles, different curves, batching, or a switch away from Groth16) that could bring this down by an order of magnitude?

“The accepted transaction lands around 100 to 120 million cycles, and the pairing check dominates by a wide margin. Multi-scalar multiplication comes next, and Molecule decoding is small next to those two.”

“Public inputs are the cost you scale directly. It’s roughly 0.28 million cycles for a small input, up to about 2.8 million for a full-width one, and there’s a practical ceiling around six public inputs that comes from the 512-byte witness buffers. Against the 3.5 billion block cycle limit, one verification at around 115 million means you fit on the order of 30 proofs in a block before anything else runs. So the real constraint is throughput, not a single proof hitting the limit.”

“On optimizations, I’ve been de-risking three. The first is batch verification, checking many proofs under one key in a single run with a randomized check. In the research spike it comes out to roughly a 79 million fixed cost plus about 19.9 million per proof, which moves you toward around 170 proofs in a block instead of 30. The second is a single-product rewrite of the on-chain verifier that saves a flat 20 million cycles or so per verification. The third is moving, proving fully into the browser, so the expensive part runs on the user’s machine instead of on-chain. The tally circuit proves in about a tenth of a second on a laptop and under two seconds on an entry-level Android phone.”

“An honest order-of-magnitude drop probably needs batching together with a cheaper verifier, and past that you’re into curve-level precompiles in CKB-VM, which is an ecosystem decision rather than something I can do alone. I’m on Groth16 largely because a working CKB verifier already exists. A different proof system is on the table long term, but it’s a bigger move.”

Trusted setup and authority model

The Private Tally treats the proof as the sole authority (no additional signature lock). You also ran a multi-party phase-2 ceremony and sealed it to a mainnet block.

What is the exact trust assumption today (how many honest contributors are required), and what is the migration path if you later want to remove the trusted setup entirely (e.g., switching to a transparent or universal SNARK that Noir can target)?

“Groth16 needs a trusted setup per circuit. For the Private Tally I ran a phase-2 ceremony with four contributors and sealed it to a public beacon, the hash of a specific CKB mainnet block (number 20,870,000) that didn’t exist when the ceremony started. The trust assumption is the standard one. The setup is sound as long as at least one of those four contributors actually discarded their secret. One honest participant is enough. I want to be clear that it’s sound if one is honest, and it isn’t an audited production ceremony.”

“Removing the trusted setup entirely means moving off per-circuit Groth16 to either a universal or updatable setup, or a fully transparent system with no setup at all. The catch cuts both ways. You need a system that Noir can target, and you need a verifier for it that’s efficient inside CKB-VM. The transparent systems tend to have larger proofs or heavier verifiers, which runs straight back into the cycle costs from the last question.”

“So it’s a real research direction rather than a committed next step. The per-circuit ceremony is the honest cost of the current design, and I’d rather be upfront that removing it isn’t free.”

Tooling direction and generated Type Scripts

What is the current scope of the generator for the type scripts (which public inputs and ell patterns are supported), and how do you plan to keep the generated binding logic auditable rather than becoming an opaque compiler output?

“That last decision is the whole auditability answer. The moment you let a spec drop into arbitrary code, the generated script becomes an opaque compiler output, and you’re back to auditing generated code line by line. By keeping the binding to a few declarative primitives, the thing a reviewer actually reads is the spec, which is short and explicit, and the generated type script follows directly from it. A linter checks the spec for unsafe patterns before anything is generated, and the generated test matrix is there to catch a binding that’s missing a check.”

“However, this is still at the research stage and the prototype has rough edges. An outside review of the spec and the linter turned up gaps that I’m fixing, which is exactly why it’s being reviewed before anything gets built on top of it. The goal isn’t to trust the generator. It’s to make the part you do have to trust small enough to actually read.”

Privacy boundaries and application surface

Which additional privacy properties are realistically achievable on CKB with the current architecture (e.g., unlinkable updates, private ownership transfer, or shielded multi-party state), and which ones would require fundamental changes to the cell model or the proof system?

“What the tally hides today is the value and every amount added, including whether an update added anything at all. What leaks is the existence of the tally, the timing of the updates, who pays the fee, and the fact that one cell’s updates are linkable to each other.”

“Taking it beyond the tally, to what the full Noir CKB architecture could realistically support once it’s built out: the core capability is private, proof-authorized state on CKB. A developer writes their rule in Noir, and the chain enforces a hidden state transition with no signature, just a proof bound to that exact transition. On top of that, the realistic next property is unlinkable updates. That needs a shielded pool, a commitment tree plus nullifiers, instead of a single cell you keep respending, so that a series of updates can’t be tied together through the cell’s history. That’s the direction I’ve been researching, and it’s also what a private ballot box needs. From there, things like private ownership transfer and shielded multi-party state become reachable on the same machinery, though they’re meaningfully harder, and I’d want the pool solid first.”

“What needs fundamental change, rather than just more circuits, is the L1 metadata. Fee payment, timing, and the existence of a transaction are visible at the chain level, and no amount of script logic hides that. You’d need network level changes, not cell model changes. So full transaction graph privacy is the wrong thing to promise on this architecture.”

“The sweet spot, for the whole thing, is any application where you want to hide a value or a state but you’re fine with the existence of the activity being public. Private counters and tallies, ballot boxes, private membership and allow lists, confidential state that a specific party updates under proof, those all fit CKB well. What I’d build elsewhere is anything that needs a large and cheap anonymity set, very high-frequency activity, or full metadata privacy. The cycle costs and the public L1 metadata make CKB the wrong tool for those, at least today. The way I think about it is that Noir CKB is for making specific pieces of state private and provably correct, not for making an entire system invisible.”

Great answers, Xiaomao! Thank you for taking the time to answer these questions. What are your next steps or plans for continued development on CKB?

“In the short term, I’m finishing the research that de-risks the hard parts, so the next things I build stand on tested ground rather than hope. The first real application I want to ship on top of that is a private ballot box, where each vote is a hidden update that the chain can count and verify without ever seeing who voted for what. Alongside that, I’m hardening the proof-to-transition binding with the generator and its test matrix.”

“I’m also contributing improvements back upstream to the Groth16 verifier that Cecilia Mulandi built, which is the on-chain verifier my whole project depends on. The main improvement is a single-product rewrite of the pairing check that cuts a flat 20 million cycles or so off every verification, along with the tighter checks that came out of reviewing it. The reason that matters is that it isn’t only my project that gets cheaper. Anyone doing Groth16 verification on CKB uses less of the block’s cycle budget, so the whole ZK stack on CKB gets a little more practical, not just Noir CKB.”

“The bigger vision is this. Right now, building a private, proof-authorized application on CKB means being both a ZK engineer and a CKB script engineer, and hand-writing the binding logic that ties a proof to an exact state transition, which is the part that’s easiest to get subtly wrong. I want to collapse that. The goal is a toolkit where a developer brings their own Noir circuit and a small, readable spec, and gets back a correct, auditable CKB type script, the artifacts, and the adversarial tests, generated for them. If that works, privacy on CKB stops being something only a handful of specialists can build, and becomes something any capable developer can reach for. That’s the thread running through everything I do, closing the gap between what the cryptography can do and what builders can actually ship. The Nervos community DAO grant work I gained after, is me building that bridge for privacy on CKB. Longer term, I want this to grow into a broader base of open privacy and ZK infrastructure and research on CKB that other people build on, not a single app that stops with me.”

Thank you, Xiaomao, for all your answers and your work among the CKB community and through the CKBuilders initiative. These interviews and projects are vital for ecosystem growth, and to help others understand CKB and the possibilities around ZK proofs.

item.title: Crossfire Loop: You Are the Bottleneck
item.dc:creator: jm9k
item.description:
How we do agentic engineering at Sōnami has evolved over the last few months. We wanted to share the “Crossfire Loop”, a method proven to yield the most favorable results for us.

Crossfire Loop: You Are the Bottleneck

Software engineering used to operate at a slower pace. Difficult architectural decisions were followed by an extended period of implementation and testing. AI is taking over the implementation and testing. Now the job of a software engineer is only the difficult parts, condensed into a non-stop, mentally taxing stream.

You are the bottleneck.

Human intellect is still required for any serious engineering task, and it is the scarcest resource. Scaling means minimizing human involvement to only what is absolutely essential.

The Crossfire Loop is the agentic engineering solution we use at Sōnami. A panel of different AI models reviews the work. The models attack each other’s findings and work together to push the work as far as it can go before a human ever looks at it.

Different Models, Different Blind Spots

Every model has strengths and weaknesses. One model is good at finding race conditions, another notices a missing test, and a third reads the spec more closely. When one model reviews its own work, it misses the same things it missed while writing.

Their blind spots differ, so a panel from different model families catches more. That has a cost. A panel uses several times the tokens of a single reviewer.

The Loop

  1. Build. The implementer writes the change. Tests must pass before any review.
  2. Review. The panel reviews the change, each model with a fresh context. They look for bugs, scope creep, and over-engineering. Extra complexity counts as a defect.
  3. Refute. More reviewers also mean more false alarms. So the same panel tries to prove each finding wrong.
  4. Judge. One judge model checks each finding against the code. Is it real? Is it in scope? Is the proposed fix over-engineered? Then it rules: fix, reject, or defer. Deferred items go to human review.
  5. Fix. The implementer fixes each accepted issue and runs the tests again.

The loop repeats until a round finds nothing serious.

Who Builds, Who Reviews

The loop has two jobs, and they need different models. The implementer writes and fixes the code. It does most of the work, so it uses most of the tokens. It must be capable, but depending on the task, a premium model can be overkill. The panel reviews. Its models must be strong, and they must come from different companies, so their blind spots differ.

Implementers

Work Model
Most Issues Most of the work is everyday features, bug fixes, and refactors. Use Claude Opus, GPT Sol, or Grok. Open-weight models also work well here: Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek, Qwen, MiniMax, etc.
Complex or Difficult Issues Architecture changes and hard-to-find bugs need the strongest implementer. Use Claude Opus or GPT Sol.
UI and Visual Work Use Claude Opus.
Long-Form Writing This includes blog posts and page content. Use Claude Opus.
Small, Non-Functional Fixes Labels, comments, and typos need little skill. Use a smaller model, such as GPT Luna or Claude Sonnet.

Panel

A normal panel has three seats: one each from Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceXAI. One seat goes to a premium model. A hard problem gets all five.

Premium models are stronger but cost much more, so they run at low effort. Even at low effort, they offer significant benefit because their baseline knowledge is much higher. The other models run at high effort. If the panel still disagrees after three rounds, another premium model joins the debate to break the tie. If the disagreement survives that, it goes to human review.

Why not only premium models? Premium models are the strongest, so one premium model, or a panel of only premium models, seems like enough. Testing shows otherwise. The lighter models still sometimes catch issues that the premium models miss, often enough to earn their seats.

Why these three companies? Open-weight models from Chinese labs add little to a panel. On reviews and hard problems, they rarely find anything that the OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceXAI models have not already found. This may be because they were distilled from models produced by these three frontier companies.

Not Just Code

The same loop works for design. One model drafts a plan, a design, or a recommendation. The panel attacks it and works toward the best version. The draft reaches a human only once nothing serious is left. The next chart started this way. Three models each proposed a design, then debated the best approach until they agreed unanimously.

What Reaches Human Review

The last column is what goes to human review. Crossfire cannot resolve everything, but the combined panel leaves far less behind. Humans still set the project direction and make the difficult decisions. Most other issues are resolved before the work reaches them.

Counting the Real Cost

Crossfire is more expensive than the usual method, where one model writes the code and a human reviews every change. Running multiple frontier models on every change means paying for multiple subscriptions, and that cost adds up fast. But the cost is a tradeoff. In return, you get fewer bugs and better code, and you move significantly faster.

An engineer’s time costs more than subscriptions. At Sōnami, the loop removes many days of unnecessary review each month for every engineer. Put a price on those days, and the subscriptions look small. In most cases, the extra cost is easily justified.

You are still the bottleneck. Crossfire makes sure your time is used only for the work that actually needs you.

The subscriptions cost money. The reviews you never have to do are worth more.

This post was originally published on the Sōnami blog: Crossfire Loop: You Are the Bottleneck | Sōnami Blog

item.title: ReuseLoop: Tracking reusable packaging lifecycles on CKB Testnet
item.dc:creator: ptt2908
item.description:
What happens to a reusable package as it moves through borrowing, return, and reuse—and what can CKB actually verify about that journey? ReuseLoop is a CKB Testnet prototype that records an item’s administrator-authorized state changes: AVAILABLE → BORROWED → RETURNED → AVAILABLE.

CKB records application state and authorized transitions. Physical handoffs, returns, cleaning, and inspections happen off-chain and are not proven by the chain.

Workflow overview

The diagram separates the current read-only walkthrough from the lifecycle modeled by the prototype.

flowchart TD
  subgraph Demo["Current walkthrough: read-only"]
    Item["Existing CKB Testnet item"] --> Read["ReuseLoop reads item state and confirmed history"]
    Read --> View["Operator sees current status and available action"]
  end

  subgraph Lifecycle["Lifecycle represented"]
    Available["AVAILABLE"] -->|Borrow| Borrowed["BORROWED"]
    Borrowed -->|Confirm return| Returned["RETURNED"]
    Returned -->|Make available| Available
  end

  Physical["Handoff, return, cleaning, inspection"] -.-> Offchain["Off-chain events are not proven by CKB state"]

How the transaction path works

An operator selects an allowed state transition and reviews its preview. One configured administrator approves it in JoyID. The app submits the signed transaction to CKB Testnet, tracks confirmation, then refreshes the item state and history.

The current walkthrough is read-only: it reuses an existing Registry and item and submits no new lifecycle transaction. CKB Lock Scripts verify the administrator’s signature; Type Scripts enforce Registry membership and valid transitions. The MVP has no separate borrower or store keys and no multi-party authorization.

Testnet evidence

The demo item completed a full lifecycle on CKB Testnet. Each link opens its confirmed transaction.

Action State Confirmed block Transaction
Item registered AVAILABLE 22,999,622 Transaction
Borrow BORROWED 22,999,649 Transaction
Confirm return RETURNED 22,999,692 Transaction
Make available AVAILABLE 22,999,731 Transaction

Repository and walkthrough

  • GitHub repository
  • Read-only Testnet walkthrough

The app currently runs locally; the project documentation does not list a hosted demo.

Verification

On 24 November 2026, the application suite passed all 62 tests across 9 files, and the production build succeeded. The minified JavaScript bundle is 799.26 kB (250.05 kB gzipped), above Vite’s 500 kB warning threshold. npm run lint currently reports three errors: synchronous state updates inside an effect in ItemLifecyclePanel.tsx and an unused err variable in ItemLookupPanel.tsx.

The Rust contract suite passed all 77 tests with no failures on 24 November 2026 (99.43 seconds). The make test helper still reports a Clang version detection warning; this run does not verify a fresh RISC-V binary build or its hash. Browser-level JoyID and RPC failure tests remain outstanding.

Feedback welcome

  1. Is a single configured administrator a reasonable authorization model for this MVP? Which roles should be added next?
  2. Is the distinction clear between on-chain state transitions and off-chain physical handling?
  3. Which failure cases, setup friction, or UX gaps should we address next?

Thanks for taking a look. I would especially value feedback on the authorization model and on how to represent physical events without overstating what the chain proves.

item.title: CKB x Kaze Unitour Phase 2 Kicks Off at Machakos University: 180+ Students, 95 New Wallets
item.dc:creator: Dorex45
item.description:
Phase 2 of the CKB x Kaze Unitour began on Thursday, 19 November at Machakos University, and the turnout exceeded what we planned for. More than 180 students joined us for three hours of hands-on learning, and 95 of them left with a brand new self-custodial wallet on Kaze.

Why we run the Unitour

Most students in Kenya have heard of Bitcoin, but very few have actually held their own keys. The Unitour exists to close that gap. We take Bitcoin and CKB education directly to campuses, and we make sure everyone leaves having done something real rather than just listened.

What we covered

The session ran from 14:00 to 17:00 and followed the same flow we use on every stop:

  • Bitcoin 101: what Bitcoin is, why it matters in Africa, and what self-custody really means
  • CKB and Nervos: the Layer 1 behind Kaze, including RGB++ and the Fiber Network
  • Kaze: how contributors earn CKB for every approved location they map, and how they can cash out to M-Pesa
  • Live wallet setup: students installed Kaze and created their own wallets in the room, step by step with our team
  • Live mapping: students added real places around campus and followed the leaderboard as pins were approved

The numbers

  • 180+ attendees
  • 95 new wallets created
  • First stop of Phase 2, following the earlier stops of the tour

What stood out

The live setup was the best part of the afternoon. Seeing a room of students create wallets at the same time, ask questions about their recovery phrases, and then start mapping places they walk past every day made the idea feel tangible. The question we heard most was how to cash out to M-Pesa, which shows how much the local offramp matters for adoption.

Challenges

No event runs perfectly, and we want to be open about what we had to solve on the day.

  • A turnout bigger than planned. We prepared for a smaller room, and more than 180 students came. A crowd that size is a good problem to have, but it stretched our space, our team and the one-on-one help we could give during wallet setup.
  • Our main videographer fell sick on the day. Our lead videographer could not make it, and with little notice we paired up with a student videographer from the university. Working from our shooting SOP guides, the student captured the raw footage, and we are sending it to our main videographer to edit into the final content. This is why highlights from the event will land a little later than usual.

Thank you

Thank you to Machakos University and the students who showed up with curiosity and energy, and to the Nervos community for the continued support behind the tour: @NervosNetwork, @ckbsamurai, @NervosNation and @ckba_build.

What’s next

The Unitour continues across Kenyan campuses. If you are a student, a club lead or a community builder and want the tour at your university, reach out to us at business@usekaze.app or on X at @usekaze. If you attended and want to keep learning, join the Kaze and CKB community groups and tell us what you want to see next.

You can download Kaze at usekaze.app.

item.dc:creator: nghiadang391
item.description:
ckb-whitehat — Spark Program application

Status: ready to run (tool shipped at v0.4.2). The repository
(https://github.com/nghiadang391/ckb-whitehat)
already exists under my GitHub account (nghiadang391) and holds two completed
pilots plus a working Go CLI release (v0.4.2, CI green). This application
funds the first systematic whitehat verification of three more CKB-DAO-funded
CKB/Fiber money products, plus three net-new forward deliverables on the tool
itself. Code for each new target lands in this repo week by week, with its
FINDINGS.md, its deterministic PoC suite, and its patch packs.

License: MIT.

Title: Spark Program | ckb-whitehat: deterministic whitehat verification of CKB/Fiber money products — AI-assisted triage, replayable PoCs, patches, consent-based disclosure

Category: DAOs & Funding → Spark Program (posted directly in the Spark sub-section per the 2026-07-19 forum update)

1. Project overview

  • Project name: ckb-whitehat
  • Repository: https://github.com/nghiadang391/ckb-whitehat (latest release: v0.4.2, MIT)
  • One-sentence summary: ckb-whitehat is a shipped community verification
    CLI (v0.4.2) with a public track record (two completed pilots, 23 findings
    — 21 PROVEN fired + 2 STRUCTURAL repo-verified); this grant funds
    applying it to three more CKB-DAO-funded CKB/Fiber money products — each
    shipped as one-command deterministic PoCs, minimal patches, and a
    consent-based disclosure record — plus three net-new tool deliverables: a
    standalone verify subcommand, a measured AI-cost reduction pass, and a
    maintainer disclosure kit.
  • Type: developer security verification tooling (already built, MIT, single
    static Go binary, zero runtime dependencies, CI green) plus a public body of
    verified findings. Developers can also run ckb-whitehat locally as a
    pre-push defensive security verification gate before shipping their own
    CKB/Fiber apps. No changes to Fiber, CKB-VM, or any grantee’s codebase;
    findings ship as PoCs + patches, applied only with the maintainer’s written
    consent.

2. Team profile

  • Nghia Dang (GitHub: nghiadang391),
    solo, all roles.
  • Contact:
    • Discord: nghia.dang.391
    • Email: nghia.dang.391@gmail.com
    • GitHub: https://github.com/nghiadang391
    • Nervos Talk: this account
  • Background: CKB ecosystem builder; author of the ckb-whitehat tool and
    methodology (https://github.com/nghiadang391/ckb-whitehat,
    MIT). Relevant public work, all verifiable in-repo:
    • Dular pilot (M-Pesa STK-push → RUSD on-ramp over Fiber; an approved
      $2,000 Spark grant, M1 verified with 3 production 1-KES deposits): 9
      findings       — F1–F7 PROVEN (fired, including 1 CRITICAL) + F8–F9
      STRUCTURAL       (verified repo inventory / pre-release lockfile pin). F1
      (“forged STK callback = free RUSD”) ends in a real CKB Pudge testnet trace
      where a fabricated KES receipt moved RUSD between two of our own local FNN
      nodes (tx hashes recorded in dular/FINDINGS.md, C4.1–C4.5). The F2
      ledger double-spend race ships with a 3-line fix and a harness that fails
      on unmodified source and passes on the fix.
    • tapfiber pilot (Fiber order/receipt library, vendored in-tree): 14
      findings (F1–F14, all PROVEN/fired)      , one-command zero-dependency
      offline PoC suite (node tapfiber/poc/attack.mjs).
    • The tool itself (v0.4.2): single static Go binary (zero runtime
      dependencies — no Node/npm needed to install; drives local authenticated
      claude, agy [Antigravity CLI], or codex CLIs in auto-detect order
      claude → agy → codex, never asking for API keys), embedded methodology,
      read-only AI-assisted init with per-command risk analysis and approval
      (setup.json handoff), live responsive 2-column TUI with one-key human
      checkpoint gates (triage / permission / publish), self-contained
      local Docker CKB devnet (nervos/ckb:v0.210.0) + 2 peered Fiber
      (nervos/fiber:0.10.1) nodes with pre-funded CKB & TEST_XUDT channels
      (ckb-whitehat chain up|status|down), mainnet refusal guard + strict
      post-run RPC hash verification, isolated Docker scratch Postgres
      (127.0.0.1:5439), 5 embedded CKB/Fiber invariant packs, broad-allow +
      strict high-risk denylist, polyglot stack support (Node, Rust/Cargo
      ckb-testtool, Go, Python), install.sh + GitHub Releases (sha256-verified
      self-update), and green CI.
  • Weekly sync: text updates in this thread, every Saturday at a fixed time
    (UTC), with the week’s findings table and repro commands.

3. Project background

The grant cycle has produced a wave of CKB/Fiber money products —
stablecoin wallets, RUSD on-ramps, Fiber-based order/receipt systems, and
CKB-script apps. Where money moves, an unauthenticated callback, a ledger
double-spend race, or an unsafe config default is directly exploitable for
asset theft. Two lanes of verification already exist:

  • Protocol-core: the CKB-VM Sail Validation Sprint and the
    ckb-verify / spark-verify acceptance-check tool cover the shared chain
    assets and the author’s own declared flows.
  • Author-side regression: a project re-running its own acceptance
    commands on a devnet.

What is missing is the adversarial, community-owned middle lane: an outside
verifier testing the default code paths of funded apps — and giving builders
a reusable pre-push verification CLI they can run locally before shipping —
with deterministic evidence a maintainer can run and trust rather than a
report of opinions. The committee has shown it values concrete, verifiable
proof: the Dular approval turned on working multi-hop RUSD payment traces plus
a clear “How to Verify” section. This application funds that same shape — a
shipped tool (v0.4.2) with public evidence, applied to three new CKB/Fiber
targets.

4. Solution

For each target, ckb-whitehat executes a fixed, reproducible pipeline:

  1. Read-only init & triage — ckb-whitehat init inspects the repo in
    strictly read-only mode to map stack dependencies and host prerequisites
    (with explicit per-command human approval for any target dependency install).
    ckb-whitehat run then maps keygen/key storage, amount parsing (BigInt vs
    Number), signing, vendor/network trust boundaries, balance/ledger
    invariants, secrets-in-config, and on-chain interactions.
  2. Named security invariant hypotheses — each names a code region, threat
    class, and the money/safety invariant it violates (no double-credit,
    non-negative balance under concurrency, callback authenticity, fail-closed
    production defaults). Ranked and scoped to what is provable locally.
  3. Deterministic PoCs — one replayable verification script per hypothesis:
    unauthenticated-webhook test, concurrent DB race harness (against isolated
    Docker scratch Postgres), config-matrix test, or boundary fuzz corpus. A
    finding ships as PROVEN only when its script actually ran against
    unmodified source and printed its captured FINDING <id> FIRED verdict.
  4. On-chain evidence — for chain-interacting targets:
    • Local deterministic devnet (--chain): self-contained Docker CKB
      devnet + 2 peered FNN v0.10.1 nodes with pre-funded CKB & TEST_XUDT
      channels (zero faucet flakiness; every reported tx/payment hash is
      automatically re-verified against local RPC by ckb-whitehat at the end
      of run).
    • Public CKB Pudge testnet (when explorer-checkable public traces add
      value):       our own 2-node FNN stack, our own addresses, faucet assets —
      impact confined strictly to our own addresses and local services. Mainnet
      is hard-refused by the CLI.
  5. Patch guidance — minimal defensive fix per finding; for races/config
    bugs, a working fixed module plus the same harness re-run proving it fails
    before and passes after.
  6. Consent-based disclosure — private report to the maintainer, patch
    window, publication only on written consent. The dated disclosure log ships
    as a deliverable so the community sees the pipeline end to end.

How the AI cost enters: steps 1–3 use the local agent CLI (claude, agy,
or codex); LLM tokens for triage, PoC engineering, and report drafting are a
real, auditable cost item budgeted explicitly in §7 (capped at $150 across all
3 targets, with per-target session logs and token counts).

5. Technical approach

  • Stack: ckb-whitehat v0.4.2 static Go binary (go test -race green in
    CI across Linux/macOS/Windows amd64/arm64) driving local claude, agy,
    or codex CLIs, plus the target’s own runtime toolchain (polyglot support:
    Node .mjs, Rust cargo test / ckb-testtool, Go, Python).
  • Local devnet & DB harness (already shipped in v0.3.x):
    • ckb-whitehat chain up boots an isolated Docker network (172.29.0.0/24)
      with nervos/ckb:v0.210.0 (127.0.0.1:8114) + 2 peered
      nervos/fiber:0.10.1 nodes (127.0.0.1:8227 / 8327), SHA-256-verified
      Fiber contracts, pre-minted genesis CKB & TEST_XUDT, and pre-opened
      ChannelReady CKB (1,000 CKB) + TEST_XUDT (100 TEST_XUDT) channels.
    • Five embedded reusable CKB/Fiber invariant packs materialized into every
      workspace (chain-client.mjs, pack-payment-idempotency.mjs,
      pack-hold-invoice-htlc.mjs, pack-udt-decimals.mjs,
      pack-self-custody.mjs).
    • Auto-provisioned isolated Docker scratch Postgres (postgres:16-alpine on
      127.0.0.1:5439, throwaway credentials) whenever a target uses Postgres.
  • Trust & safety boundaries:
    • Untrusted target isolation: --setting-sources user (Claude), no
      --add-dir <target> (agy, blocking untrusted .agents/hooks.json),
      project_doc_max_bytes=0 (Codex), hardened git clone (hooksPath=/dev/null,
      fsmonitor=false, symlinks=false), and workspace-confined cwd.
    • Broad safe tool allowlist paired with a strict high-risk denylist blocking
      rm -rf, git push, git reset --hard, sudo, curl, wget, ssh,
      psql, env, live web fetches, MCP, and target-repo writes.
    • Mainnet refusal guard (VerifyMainnetSafe) checks CKB get_blockchain_info
      and FNN chain_hash before any --chain run.
    • External third-party vendors (M-Pesa/Daraja, webhooks, external APIs) are
      always mocked/stubbed locally; no live service is ever probed.
  • Hard parts:
    • Keeping every PoC deterministic and one-command reproducible against
      unmodified source across heterogeneous stacks (JS/TS, Rust CKB-scripts,
      Go).
    • Separating app-layer bugs from chain/FNN behavior in every recorded
      on-chain state transition (linking upstream protocol issues rather than
      claiming them as app findings).
    • Managing responsible disclosure timelines while keeping pre-consent
      details private and still giving the committee an auditable dated log.
  • Language: English.

6. To-Do list (6 weeks)

The CLI (v0.4.2) and local CKB/Fiber devnet + scratch Postgres harness are
already built and proven on two pilots. The funded work is: (a) applying
ckb-whitehat to three new CKB-DAO-funded CKB/Fiber money products, and (b)
three net-new forward deliverables on the tool itself.

  • Week 1: D1 target selection posted in-thread (3 CKB-DAO-funded CKB/Fiber
    projects from the active Spark/CKB registry, at least one a money product:
    wallet / on-ramp / exchange / payment tool), with rationale and overlap check
    against Sail-validation and author-side regression lanes. Verify local
    devnet (ckb-whitehat chain up) + baseline green trace for Target 1 (and
    optional Pudge testnet trace if public explorer verification applies).
    • Milestone: targets named and unchallenged for 7 days.
  • Week 2: Target 1, complete pack: offline findings + PoC suite + patch
    guidance, local devnet / on-chain evidence (recorded hashes verified against
    RPC), first private disclosure contact sent.
    • Milestone: Target 1 pack reproducible with one command per finding;
      disclosure #1 sent.
  • Week 3: Target 2, complete pack + disclosure #2 sent.
  • Week 4: Target 3, complete pack + disclosure #3 sent.
    • Milestone: all three target packs merged to the repo, CI green.
  • Week 5: Net-new forward work (D6), three shippable PRs:
    1. Standalone ckb-whitehat verify <FINDINGS.md> subcommand: unlike
      v0.4.2’s in-run post-check, this standalone subcommand lets any
      committee reviewer or maintainer re-audit an already published
      FINDINGS.md with zero LLM calls — re-running its PoC suite and
      re-verifying recorded tx/payment hashes against local devnet or Pudge
      testnet RPC. Turns “How to Verify” into a single binary command.
    2. Measured AI-cost reduction pass: establish a logged Week-1 token/cost
      baseline per target, then cut total token spend via structured per-run
      usage telemetry, prompt caching of the triage pass, tiered/smaller models
      for mechanical checks, tighter gate-loop budgeting, and a hashed
      known-issue catalog       (recording deterministic (step, exit_code, error_class) hashes — never raw untrusted target output — mapped to
      curated remedies so repeated environment failures short-circuit with zero
      LLM turns and log recovered-known-issue <sig>). Target: ≥ 40% token
      reduction       vs. baseline while still firing every finding on re-run.
    3. 1-page quickstart + maintainer disclosure kit: a concise quickstart
      for developers running ckb-whitehat pre-push on their own repo, plus
      the exact public maintainer disclosure letter template and consent
      checklist.
      Cross-target SUMMARY.md (finding taxonomy, recurring foot-guns,
      recommended community fixes) drafted alongside.
  • Week 6: Full regression re-run of every PoC against unmodified source;
    secret-material sweep (confirming zero real provider keys, OTPs, phone PII,
    or CKB hex keys in PoCs/reports); completion report with funds-usage vs. §7;
    captioned 3-minute walkthrough demo of one full target run from init
    through fired PoC and verified on-chain trace.
    • Milestone: final deliverable set live; ckb-whitehat verify green in CI.

7. Required funding & funding breakdown

Total: $950 USD, paid in CKB (within the standard $1,000 single-category
budget tier).

( English below )

这是什么？为什么要做在 CKB 上？

CellCat 是一个跑在 CKB 上的全链上基因猫小游戏，玩法很简单：领养 → 配对产蛋 → 等出块孵化 → 挂单交易 / 熔猫。

选 CKB 带来的特性：

  • 猫有真地板价：每只猫都是一个真实的 Cell，喂食就是往里存 CKB；不想玩了随时“熔猫”，Cell 里的 CKB 全退回钱包。
  • 不存图，链上算基因：每只猫只存 32 字节 DNA（显性+隐性基因），繁殖先产蛋、到指定块高取区块头做随机源，链上重算 DNA 防作弊。
  • 无托管原子交易：用 sale-lock 挂单，买家付够 CKB 直接换锁成交，卖家随时撤单，不需要把猫转给平台托管。
  • 零门槛：接入 JoyID，不用装插件背助记词，打开网页就能玩。

目前已经做完的部分（本地 Devnet 已跑通）

  • 4 个 Rust 合约（cat-type、egg-type、sale-lock、config-type）：纯手写字节布局和 ckb_std::syscalls，避开了 riscv64imac 原子指令的坑。
  • 跨端基因库：Rust（no_std）和前端 JS 逐字节一致，有 82 条自动化校验向量。
  • 合约测试：ckb-testtool 写了 20 多个正常和异常用例（防改 DNA、冷却、次数上限、繁育费、区块头、挂单少付/错付等），已全过。
  • 移动端网页：猫舍、繁育、集市、明信片生成和基础社交交互在本地 devnet 上已经能玩。

开发规划

  • 第 1 周：完善玩法机制；美化视觉资产；复查合约的边界；测试经济学可持续性；部署到 CKB Testnet 。做数据统计 dashboard。
  • 第 2 周：上公网 HTTPS 服务器，小范围拉 20–50 个内测玩家，实测领养、繁殖孵化、买卖、喂食和熔猫全流程。
  • 第 3 周：内测收尾，发放激励，汇总反馈。进一步完善代码。
  • 第 4 周：接通 JoyID（Testnet）。交付代码、演示录屏。

验收

  1. 直接玩：打开公网链接，用 JoyID 领猫、配种、等孵化、去集市挂单/买猫、熔掉退回 CKB，全流程可以体验验证。
  2. 查浏览器：结项时我会把 4 个合约的部署哈希，以及领养、繁殖、孵化、成交、熔猫的 Testnet 交易哈希全贴出来啊。 ，直接在 Explorer 上对账。
  3. 看录屏：附一段 2 分钟无剪辑实操录屏。
  4. 跑源码测试：拉下仓库直接在本地或者服务器部署运行

预算：$680

项目 说明 金额
人工工时 30 小时 × $15/小时 $450
AI Token 编码 + 排查测试 + 猫猫部件美术素材优化 $100
内测用户激励 发给参与完整测试和报有效 Bug 的社区玩家（规则和转账记录全公开） $100
服务器 云服务器 + 域名/HTTPS（覆盖内测及结项展示） $30
合计 $680

关于我

简介：业余全栈开发，ckb123.com（已下线）站长，CKB 主网启动参与者之一

GitHub： cool007zqw (Enzo Zheng) · GitHub 大部分项目涉及工作或个人信息因此没有设为公开可见

联系：请直接通过 Nervos Talk 联络

What Is This, and Why Build It on CKB?

CellCat is a fully on-chain genetic cat game built on CKB. The gameplay is simple: Adopt → Breed to produce eggs → Wait for block-based hatching → List for sale or burn cats.

Why CKB?

Real floor value for every cat: Each cat is represented by a real Cell. Feeding a cat means depositing CKB into its Cell. If you no longer want to play, you can simply “burn” the cat and recover all the CKB stored in its Cell back to your wallet.

No images stored on-chain; genetics are computed on-chain: Each cat stores only 32 bytes of DNA (dominant + recessive genes). Breeding first produces an egg. Once a designated block height is reached, the block header is used as a randomness source, and the DNA is recomputed on-chain to prevent cheating.

Non-custodial atomic trading: Cats are listed using sale-lock. Buyers can complete a purchase by paying the required amount of CKB and unlocking the transaction directly. Sellers can cancel their listings at any time. Cats never need to be transferred to a platform for custody.

Zero-friction onboarding: Integrated with JoyID. No browser extensions or seed phrases required. Just open the website and start playing.

The entire system has been successfully tested on a local Devnet.

Smart contracts

  • Four Rust contracts implemented: “cat-type”, “egg-type”, “sale-lock”, and “config-type”.
  • Handwritten byte layouts and “ckb_std::syscalls” are used to avoid issues with unsupported atomic instructions in “riscv64imac”.

Cross-platform genetics library

  • The Rust (“no_std”) and frontend JavaScript implementations produce byte-for-byte identical results.
  • 82 automated test vectors are in place to verify consistency.

Smart contract testing

  • More than 20 test cases implemented using “ckb-testtool”, covering both normal and edge cases.
  • Test coverage includes DNA tampering prevention, cooldowns, breeding limits, breeding fees, block header validation, and underpayment/incorrect payment during marketplace transactions.
  • All tests are passing.

Mobile-friendly web application

  • The cattery, breeding system, marketplace, postcard generation, and basic social interactions are all playable on the local Devnet.

  • Finalize gameplay mechanics.
  • Polish visual assets.
  • Review smart contract edge cases.
  • Evaluate the economic sustainability of the game.
  • Deploy to CKB Testnet.
  • Build a data analytics dashboard.

Week 2:

  • Launch a public HTTPS server.
  • Recruit 20–50 players for a small closed beta.
  • Test the complete user journey, including adoption, breeding, hatching, trading, feeding, and burning cats.

Week 3:

  • Wrap up the closed beta.
  • Distribute participation incentives.
  • Collect and review user feedback.
  • Further improve the codebase.

Week 4:

  • Integrate JoyID on Testnet.
  • Deliver the source code and a recorded demonstration.

Acceptance Criteria

  1. Play the game directly

Open the public URL and use JoyID to adopt cats, breed them, wait for eggs to hatch, list or purchase cats on the marketplace, and burn cats to recover their CKB. The entire gameplay loop will be publicly accessible and verifiable.

  1. Verify on the blockchain

At project completion, I will publish the deployment transaction hashes of all four smart contracts, along with the Testnet transaction hashes for adoption, breeding, hatching, successful trades, and cat burning.

Everything can be independently verified and reconciled directly through the CKB Explorer.

  1. Watch an unedited demo

A two-minute, unedited screen recording demonstrating the actual gameplay will be provided.

  1. Run the source code and tests

Clone the repository and deploy and run the project locally or on your own server.

item.title: Spark Program | FiberVPN: Pay-Per-Hour WireGuard Tunnels over Fiber
item.dc:creator: akanjacson
item.description:
Project: FiberVPN
Applicant: Akan Theodore (kd-designs on GitHub: GitHub - kd-designs/fibervpn: Pay-per-hour and pay-per-MB WireGuard VPN exit gateway powered by Nervos Fiber Network · GitHub )
Funding requested: $750 USD equivalent in CKB (payout address shared on approval)
Timeline: 5 weeks
Contact: Nervos Talk DM

What FiberVPN Is

FiberVPN is a self-hosted WireGuard exit gateway and browser checkout that sells encrypted VPN tunnels by the hour or by the megabyte over Nervos Fiber Network.

You open the web page, pick a tier (1 hour / 500 MB or 24 hours / 5 GB), pay a Fiber invoice and get a WireGuard QR code and .conf file immediately. You scan it into the official WireGuard app on your phone or laptop, route traffic through the exit node and get disconnected cleanly as soon as the paid time or byte quota hits zero

Why Build This

Most commercial VPNs force users into $10+/month subscriptions, email signups or credit card billing just to get encrypted internet on airport, hotel or cafe Wi-Fi for an afternoon. On Bitcoin Lightning, LNVPN showed that pay-as-you-go WireGuard tunnels are one of the few micropayment apps people actually return to use.

FiberVPN brings that same pattern to Fiber without accounts or custodial logins:

  • The browser generates the WireGuard keypair locally and persists it in localStorage so refreshing the tab while waiting for payment never orphans a paid tunnel.
  • The backend validates the Curve25519 public key, creates a Fiber invoice via fnn (new_invoice) and allocates a tunnel IP only after get_invoice reports Paid.
  • Every 10 seconds, the quota daemon checks wg show wg0 transfer and tears down any peer whose paid duration or byte limit is reached, recycling its IP back into the /24 pool.

How it sits next to other Fiber projects: MeterNet meters local router Wi-Fi per megabyte via openNDS captive-portal rules, while Fiber Paid HTTP gates single HTTP requests behind payment headers. Neither gives a remote user an OS-level encrypted WireGuard tunnel they can turn on from anywhere using the standard WireGuard app.

How It Works

Browser generates WireGuard keypair locally (saved in localStorage)
  -> sends publicKey + tier to FiberVPN gateway
  -> gateway validates Curve25519 key, calls fnn new_invoice and returns invoice

User pays invoice (~1s via Fiber wallet or @nervosnetwork/fiber-js WASM)
  -> gateway sees Paid via get_invoice
  -> allocates IP from /24 pool -> runs `wg set wg0 peer <pubkey> allowed-ips <ip>/32`
  -> browser injects local PrivateKey and renders WireGuard QR / .conf

Quota daemon (every 10s, backed by SQLite)
  -> reads `wg show wg0 transfer`
  -> on expiry or rx+tx >= maxBytes, runs `wg set wg0 peer <pubkey> remove` and recycles IP

The HTTP server runs unprivileged (not as root), scoped via CAP_NET_ADMIN / sudoers strictly to wg set wg0 and wg show wg0 transfer with execFile and zero shell interpolation. During the public testnet trial, nftables forwarding on wg0 blocks outbound SMTP (25, 465, 587) and BitTorrent while leaving standard web, SSH and DNS ports (80, 443, 53) open so testers cannot get the VPS flagged for spam.

For reviewers who do not run a local fnn node, Week 2 puts a public testnet web MVP online with a built-in @nervosnetwork/fiber-js browser WASM flow alongside the raw invoice QR. You fund from the testnet faucet, pay a 15 min / 50 MB test tier right in your browser, scan the WireGuard QR on your phone or laptop and confirm your public IP switches to the exit node and cuts off at expiry.

Applicant Background

I’m Akan Theodore (kd-designs), an independent full-stack developer working mostly with TypeScript, Node.js services and Linux networking. I haven’t run a public fnn node before, so Week 1 tackles live Pudge testnet channel opening and wg set peer provisioning on a Linux VPS up front before building the browser UI on top of it.

What Already Exists vs. What the Grant Funds

An initial v0.1.0 core is already written in TypeScript ( GitHub - kd-designs/fibervpn: Pay-per-hour and pay-per-MB WireGuard VPN exit gateway powered by Nervos Fiber Network · GitHub ) and runs locally today:

  • Curve25519 base64 key validation rejecting malformed or shell-injected keys (src/wireguard.ts)
  • /24 IP pool allocator (IpPoolAllocator), .conf builder and WgCliAdapter using execFile('wg', ...)
  • FnnRpcClient wired to FNN’s new_invoice and get_invoice JSON-RPC schema plus an in-memory mock (src/fiber-rpc.ts)
  • VpnManager with post-payment IP allocation, concurrent activation locking, duplicate-active-key protection and automatic time/byte quota cutoffs (src/manager.ts)
  • 8 passing unit tests (npm test) and a local simulation (npm run demo)

What this grant funds (5 weeks):

  • Live Linux + WireGuard + fnn gateway: Provisioning wg0 NAT/forwarding, nftables port filtering and a funded Pudge testnet fnn node on a public Linux VPS.
  • Public browser MVP (Week 2): Hosted testnet page with client-side Curve25519 keygen (localStorage-backed), @nervosnetwork/fiber-js WASM checkout alongside raw invoice QRs and WireGuard QR rendering.
  • SQLite persistence & restart reconciliation (Week 3): Persisting sessions and byte checkpoints in SQLite so daemon restarts clean up peers that expired offline and never reset wg byte counters.
  • 14-day public testnet trial & verifier (Weeks 4-5): Opening the testnet exit node to Nervos Talk testers for two weeks, publishing a standalone status/verification CLI (npx fibervpn status <payment_hash>), recording an unedited mobile WireGuard demo video and posting the closing report with testnet payment hashes and honest latency/failure notes.

Deliverables & Timeline

  • Week 1: Live wg0 + fnn testnet node: Linux VPS running WireGuard wg0, nftables rules and a funded Pudge testnet fnn node; first real invoice-to-peer-add test passed
  • Week 2: Public testnet web MVP: Hosted demo URL posted on this thread with browser @nervosnetwork/fiber-js + QR checkout, WireGuard QR generation and live peer status board.
  • Week 3: Persistence & quota cutoff suite: SQLite session recovery across restarts and live cutoff tests for both time expiry and byte-cap exhaustion.
  • Weeks 4-5: 14-day community trial, CLI & wrap-up: Two weeks of public testnet usage, verification CLI published, unedited mobile WireGuard cutoff video recorded and closing report posted.

Budget: $750 USD in CKB

Priced by milestone (no VPS hardware or hosting fees billed separately):

  • Week 1 ($150): Linux VPS wg0 setup, nftables rules and testnet fnn channel liquidity
  • Week 2 ($200): Public testnet web MVP, client-side keygen, WASM checkout and WireGuard QR UI
  • Week 3 ($200): SQLite persistence, restart reconciliation and automated quota cutoff tests
  • Weeks 4-5 ($200): 14-day public trial, verification CLI, walkthrough video and closing report

How Anyone Can Verify

  1. Right now (local repo): Clone GitHub - kd-designs/fibervpn: Pay-per-hour and pay-per-MB WireGuard VPN exit gateway powered by Nervos Fiber Network · GitHub , run npm install && npm test && npm run demo to verify the 8 tests, key validation, concurrency guard and quota cutoff simulation.
  2. From Week 2: Open the live testnet URL, pay a testnet Fiber invoice via the browser WASM flow (or your own Fiber node), scan the WireGuard QR in the official WireGuard app, check ifconfig.me before and after connecting and watch traffic stop at expiry.
  3. At completion: Run npx fibervpn status <payment_hash> against our public logs and watch the unedited phone-to-WireGuard walkthrough video.

Maintenance

For 6 months after completion, I will keep fibervpn updated against fnn JSON-RPC changes and answer setup issues on GitHub within 48 hours.

item.title: Sigsheet: one file for signing CKB multisig transactions across ckb-cli, Neuron and CCC apps (first spec draft, feedback wanted)
item.dc:creator: ILE_LABS
item.description:
Hi everyone,

We’ve published the first draft of Sigsheet, an open file format for signing a CKB multisig transaction. Each signer uses the wallet they already have: ckb-cli, Neuron, or an app built on CCC. We’d like your feedback before we write the implementations.

The problem

A CKB multisig transaction is usually signed by several people, often with different tools. Today two things get in the way.

  • Partial signatures don’t travel between tools. ckb-cli, Neuron, CCC and ckb-sdk each hold a partly signed multisig transaction in a different way. The incompatibility between ckb-cli’s tx file and Neuron was reported in 2024 (ckb-cli#584, neuron#3048). In our tests with ckb-cli 2.0.0, Neuron 0.204.1 and CCC 1.23.1, none of the three read another’s partial signatures: they were dropped on import, lost silently, or the file couldn’t be read at all (the measurements). So in practice, one person collects everyone’s signatures and assembles the transaction. Fiber’s 0.7.0 mainnet script upgrade this month, for example, gathered four of its five signatures from pull request comments (fiber-scripts#34).
  • A signature doesn’t cover the input cells. The multisig lock signs the transaction hash and the witnesses, and the transaction hash covers each input’s out point, not the cell it points to. A signer who can’t see the input cells can’t check the amounts they are signing.

What Sigsheet is

One canonical JSON file per transaction. It carries:

  • the transaction, with a witness template for each lock group to be signed;
  • the previous transaction of every input, so a reader checks every input cell offline, by hash;
  • the block headers and inclusion proofs a Nervos DAO withdrawal needs;
  • the multisig configs;
  • every signature so far, keyed by lock group and signer.

How it’s used:

  • Signers pass the file along, or each one shares a copy and anyone merges them. Any order gives the same bytes.
  • Whoever holds a ready file finalizes it into a standard transaction.
  • It works with the multisig locks and addresses already on chain: the genesis, 2024 and v2 deployments. There’s no new on-chain script.

The goal

One file that every signer’s tool reads and writes: apps built on CCC through a TypeScript library, any Rust tool through a Rust library, and the official ckb-cli and Neuron through one Sigsheet tool until they read it themselves. Wallets don’t talk to each other through it: every wallet writes to the same file, and nobody has to collect and forward signatures.

What’s published

All of this is in github.com/ILE-Labs/Sigsheet, linked at commits 4588a55 on main and e4896d3 on research so every comment refers to a known version:

  • The specification, first draft. It covers:

    • the file and its canonical form;
    • 31 reader checks, all run offline;
    • the message rule of each lock;
    • merge, ready and finalize, including a rule for the signature sets the genesis multisig binary rejects;
    • what a signer is shown;
    • creating and sending;
    • security considerations.

    Every rule links to its evidence.

  • Test vectors: 24 cases, 18 attacks and 2 mainnet transactions, rebuilt byte for byte by one command.

  • An independent check:

    • every message is recomputed with CCC’s and ckb-cli’s own code;
    • every signature is recovered;
    • every final transaction runs through the deployed lock binaries under ckb-debugger.

    The checks run on Linux, macOS and Windows.

  • The design record and its benchmarks, on the repository’s research branch:

    • every decision, with its evidence;
    • the paths considered, and why each was dropped;
    • the experiments.

What we’ve learned since publishing

  • On ckb-devrel/ccc#646, CCC’s maintainer closed the request: CCC currently has no plans to include Sigsheet, and further progress is welcome here on Nervos Talk. So we’re building it as a separate package on @ckb-ccc/core as published, with no change to CCC. The thread also asked why a new format is needed at all; the first question below answers it.
  • We’ve also shared it with ckb-cli’s and Neuron’s maintainers (ckb-cli#694, neuron#3518).

Two questions we’ve already been asked

  • Why not keep the partial signatures in the transaction itself? We tested that as our path D, and two design-stage measurements on Fiber’s 0.7.0 upgrade (a 3-of-5 multisig whose members sent five signatures) moved us off it. A witness with M slots can’t keep the signatures beyond M, and merging the five copies inside the witness in all 120 orders gave 60 different results (X3a, section 1). Sigsheet keeps every signature by lock group and signer: its merge gave the same result in 2,000 of 2,000 trials (X3a, section 2), and finalizes to the standard transaction (why path D was dropped).
  • Why not a hosted multisig wallet? A hosted wallet removes the exchange when every member uses it. Sigsheet is for groups whose members sign with different tools, such as ckb-cli and Neuron, on any of the three multisig deployments. A service like that could also read and write the same file.

What’s next: the roadmap to v1.0

  • v0.1:
    • the specification after this feedback;
    • a TypeScript library on CCC, the reference implementation;
    • a Rust library;
    • one Sigsheet tool for signers, which signs with the official ckb-cli and Neuron through their own export files;
    • a demo on testnet with all three tools.
  • v0.2:
    • a readable summary for signers;
    • a command that writes the file and that summary in one step, in the Sigsheet tool and offered to ckb-cli;
    • an optional relay that carries one signature at a time, about 367 bytes at design stage, instead of the whole file;
    • Neuron’s own Sigsheet screens;
    • Omnilock’s multisig mode;
    • support in more tools.
  • v1.0: a stable specification with a conformance suite any implementation can run, proposed as a CKB RFC.

None of this depends on any project including the changes:

  • the TypeScript library will work with CCC as published;
  • ckb-cli and Neuron users sign with the official wallets, through the Sigsheet tool.

At design stage, each wallet’s change was small:

  • 381 code lines in ckb-cli, 229 in CCC and 137 in Neuron;
  • each wallet’s own tests gave the same results before and after (X6);
  • on a local devnet, ckb-cli, CCC and Neuron signed one shared file in seven flows, all committed (X5).

The feedback we’re looking for

  • If you sign multisig transactions today, for a treasury, a team wallet or script deployments: which tools do your members sign with, and which transactions? We’ll make sure the first implementations cover them, and once they exist we’d like to run one of yours through Sigsheet with you, on testnet.
  • Wallet and SDK maintainers: what would your signing flow need from the format?
  • Security reviewers:
    • the reader checks (§5);
    • the signature rules (§7);
    • the attacks considered (§13).
  • CoBuild and CKB IDL: the boundary in Annexes A and B.

@quake, @phroi: Fiber’s 0.7.0 upgrade, which you both took part in, gathered its five signatures from the deploy file and four pull request comments. It’s the case we most want to get right. A whole Sigsheet file for that upgrade is about 733 KB at design stage, far more than a signature in a comment. So v0.2 adds a ckb-cli command that writes the file in one step, and a relay message of one signature, about 367 bytes. Your view on how signatures should travel in that flow would help most. @doitian: the request-signature step you planned for ckb-cli deploy (ckb-cli#603) is the job we want Sigsheet’s file to do, and your view on what it needs would help too. @RetricSu, @rink1969: you’ve signed multisig transactions with ckb-cli and Neuron and run into their limits (ckb-cli#658, neuron#3260), and we’d value your view of the draft.

Every change the feedback leads to will be listed in the repository with specification v0.1, and linked from this thread.

Thanks for reading. We’ll answer every comment here.

— ILE Labs
