item.title: Unlinked for CKB: Tor-Routed RPC and Browser Privacy Extension
item.dc:creator: Owais
item.description:
Funding requested: $1,000
Project duration: 6 weeks
Category: Developer Tools / Privacy
Target ecosystem: Nervos CKB
License: Open source

Applicant: Owais (GitHub: owaisdotcom) · Full Stack Software Engineer

1. Project Overview

Unlinked for CKB is an open-source browser extension prototype designed to improve privacy when interacting with Nervos CKB decentralized applications.

It adapts the anon-rpc architecture and browser-based Tor client (tor-js, based on Arti compiled to WebAssembly) to the CKB ecosystem. The goal is to let users route supported CKB RPC requests through Tor directly from their browser, without requiring them to install or operate a separate native Tor daemon.

The extension will investigate running the privacy worker in a sandboxed browser environment and integrating it with CKB RPC endpoints to provide Tor-routed blockchain access.

The prototype will implement two complementary features:

  1. Tor-Routed CKB RPC: A browser-compatible transport that routes supported CKB RPC requests through the Tor network, reducing the ability of RPC endpoints to associate requests with a user’s direct IP address.
  2. Wallet Privacy Inspector: A browser-based inspection tool that detects CKB addresses and recognizable wallet-related information in outgoing requests and shows users which external domains receive that information.

The project will focus on building a functional prototype rather than a production-ready privacy service. It will adapt existing technologies, develop the CKB-specific integration, test both features in real browser environments, and publish the resulting software with documentation and demonstrations.

The goal is to give CKB developers and users an early, usable example of browser-level privacy tooling, while providing a foundation for further development in the Nervos ecosystem.

2. Problem Statement

When users interact with CKB dApps, information can be exposed through both network connections and application-generated browser requests.

Network-level exposure

When a browser communicates directly with a CKB RPC provider, that provider can observe the connecting IP address. Changing RPC providers does not necessarily prevent this exposure.

Tor offers a way to route network connections through multiple relays, making it harder for the destination endpoint to associate requests with the user’s direct IP address. However, browser networking restrictions make a browser-native implementation challenging.

Wallet information disclosure

A dApp may transmit CKB addresses or other recognizable wallet information to external services through browser requests. These services can include analytics providers, application APIs and other third-party endpoints.

Users generally have little visibility into which domains receive this information.

Unlinked aims to address these two problems through a browser extension that provides experimental private RPC access and local inspection of outgoing wallet-related information.

3. Why Nervos CKB?

CKB’s Cell model and Lock Script architecture provide recognizable structures that can be used when inspecting wallet-related information.

CKB addresses encode information about locking scripts and their arguments. This gives the privacy inspector a practical starting point for detecting CKB-related identifiers in outgoing requests.

The prototype will investigate how to recognize these structures without accessing private keys or uploading users’ browsing data.

CKB also has an ecosystem of wallets, dApps and RPC-based applications that provides a relevant environment for developing and testing browser privacy tooling.

The project complements existing CKB infrastructure. A Light Client can independently verify blockchain data, while Tor addresses network-level IP exposure. These are different capabilities, and the prototype focuses on exploring the latter alongside wallet information inspection.

4. Proposed Prototype

Unlinked for CKB will consist of a browser extension with two main experimental features.

4.1 Tor-Routed CKB RPC

The first feature will prototype browser-compatible access to CKB RPC endpoints through Tor.

The intended request path is:

Browser extension → Tor-compatible transport → Tor network → CKB RPC endpoint

The prototype will investigate existing browser-compatible Tor technologies, including Arti-based WebAssembly approaches where practical.

Initial development will focus on:

  • Establishing a browser-compatible Tor transport.
  • Connecting to a configurable CKB RPC endpoint.
  • Routing a defined set of CKB JSON-RPC requests through Tor.
  • Displaying connection and routing status in the extension.
  • Handling connection failures without silently falling back to a direct connection.

The objective is to demonstrate that a browser extension can make supported CKB RPC requests without exposing the user’s direct IP address to the destination endpoint.

The initial prototype will use existing Tor technologies rather than attempt to implement the Tor protocol from scratch.

If an external gateway or relay is required, its role and operational dependencies will be documented.

4.2 Wallet Privacy Inspector

The second feature will prototype local inspection of outgoing browser requests to identify CKB wallet-related information.

The initial version will inspect Fetch and XMLHttpRequest traffic.

It will attempt to detect:

  • CKB addresses.
  • Recognizable Lock Script arguments.
  • Other identifiable CKB wallet-related values.
  • External domains receiving detected information.

The extension will display findings in a per-site privacy report.

For example, when a dApp sends a user’s CKB address to an external analytics endpoint, the extension will identify the destination domain and show the detected information.

The inspector will operate locally in the browser. It will not upload inspected request contents to a central service.

The initial prototype will focus on Fetch and XMLHttpRequest. WebSocket and other traffic types may be explored later, but will not be required for the first version.

5. Prototype Architecture

Browser extension

The main interface will provide connection controls, privacy inspection and per-site reports.

Tor transport

A browser-compatible Tor transport will be integrated for supported CKB RPC requests. The implementation will evaluate available WebAssembly and browser networking approaches.

CKB RPC integration

The extension will connect to a configurable CKB RPC endpoint and support a defined subset of JSON-RPC methods.

Request inspection

The inspector will analyze observable Fetch and XMLHttpRequest requests for recognizable CKB wallet information and associate findings with destination domains.

Local privacy reporting

Inspection results will be presented locally, without sending browsing or wallet information to a central analytics service.

6. Development Deliverables

The project will produce:

  1. Browser extension prototype: An installable, open-source extension containing the initial privacy features.
  2. Tor-Routed RPC prototype: A working browser-based experiment for routing supported CKB RPC requests through Tor, subject to transport feasibility.
  3. Wallet Privacy Inspector: A working prototype that detects CKB addresses and recognizable wallet information in outgoing requests.
  4. Per-site privacy report: An interface displaying detected wallet information and destination domains.
  5. CKB dApp test environment: A controlled test dApp demonstrating wallet information disclosure and inspection.
  6. Existing dApp compatibility tests: Tests against at least two existing CKB applications, documenting supported behavior and observed results.
  7. Source code and documentation: Public repository, setup instructions, technical notes and a demonstration video.

7. Six-Week Development Plan

Week 1 — Extension Foundation and Tor Setup

  • Set up the browser extension project.
  • Investigate browser-compatible Tor transport options.
  • Evaluate Arti-based WebAssembly approaches.
  • Configure a CKB RPC test environment.
  • Define the initial RPC methods to support.

Milestone: Extension foundation and initial Tor transport experiment.

Week 2 — Tor-Routed RPC Prototype

  • Implement the initial browser-compatible transport.
  • Attempt to connect to a CKB RPC endpoint through Tor.
  • Add connection status and error handling.
  • Test routing behavior and prevent silent direct-connection fallback.

Milestone: Initial Tor-routed CKB RPC prototype, or documented technical limitations and an alternative implementation approach.

Week 3 — Wallet Privacy Inspector

  • Implement Fetch and XMLHttpRequest inspection.
  • Add CKB address detection.
  • Investigate recognizable Lock Script argument detection.
  • Identify destination domains.
  • Build the initial privacy report interface.

Milestone: Functional wallet information inspection prototype.

Week 4 — CKB dApp Integration and Testing

  • Build a controlled CKB test dApp.
  • Test the inspector against controlled wallet-information disclosures.
  • Integrate at least two existing CKB dApps into the testing process.
  • Record observed requests and findings.
  • Improve detection and reporting.

Milestone: Working inspection demonstration and initial compatibility results.

Week 5 — Prototype Integration

  • Integrate the working components into the browser extension.
  • Test supported CKB RPC requests.
  • Verify Tor routing behavior where implemented.
  • Improve the extension interface.
  • Address compatibility and performance issues.

Milestone: Integrated Unlinked for CKB prototype.

Week 6 — Final Testing and Release

  • Complete functional tests.
  • Fix remaining issues.
  • Publish the source code.
  • Write setup and developer documentation.
  • Publish the CKB dApp testing results.
  • Record a demonstration video.

Milestone: Public prototype release.

8. Success Metrics and Verification

The project will be evaluated through working software and reproducible demonstrations.

Tor-Routed RPC

  • Demonstrate a supported CKB RPC request routed through Tor in a real browser, if technically feasible.
  • Verify that the destination endpoint observes the Tor exit IP rather than the user’s direct IP.
  • Display routing status in the extension.
  • Demonstrate that the extension does not silently fall back to a direct connection.

Wallet Privacy Inspector

  • Detect CKB addresses in controlled outgoing requests.
  • Identify destination domains.
  • Display detected information in a per-site report.
  • Demonstrate local inspection without uploading request contents.

CKB Application Testing

  • Test at least two existing CKB dApps.
  • Document observed wallet-information disclosures and negative findings.
  • Publish reproducible test cases.

Open-Source Release

  • Publish the extension source code.
  • Provide installation and setup instructions.
  • Publish a demonstration and technical documentation.

The project will clearly distinguish implemented functionality from experimental or unsupported features.

9. Risks and Mitigations

Browser-compatible Tor transport

Browser networking restrictions may make direct Tor integration difficult.

Mitigation: Use existing browser-compatible Tor technologies, limit the initial implementation to supported RPC requests and document transport limitations.

Incomplete request inspection

Some wallet information may be encoded or transmitted through unsupported traffic types.

Mitigation: Focus the initial prototype on observable Fetch and XMLHttpRequest requests and document unsupported mechanisms.

False positives and missed disclosures

Not every detected string necessarily represents a privacy leak, and transformed data may not be recognizable.

Mitigation: Validate detections against controlled test cases and distinguish confirmed findings from potential disclosures.

10. Funding Request

Total requested: $1,000

The funding will support six weeks of prototype development, integration and testing.

The budget covers:

  • Browser extension development.
  • Tor transport integration and experimentation.
  • CKB RPC integration.
  • Wallet Privacy Inspector development.
  • User interface and reporting.
  • CKB dApp testing.
  • Documentation, open-source publication and demonstration.

The resulting software and technical documentation will be publicly available to the Nervos ecosystem.

11. Expected Ecosystem Impact

Unlinked for CKB will introduce an experimental browser privacy tool for the Nervos ecosystem.

For users, it aims to provide greater visibility into wallet-related information transmitted by dApps and demonstrate an alternative way to access supported CKB RPC endpoints.

For developers, it will provide a practical example of browser-based wallet information inspection and a test environment for evaluating application privacy.

For the wider ecosystem, it will contribute:

  • An open-source browser extension prototype.
  • Experimental Tor integration for CKB RPC access.
  • A reusable wallet privacy inspection component.
  • Testing results from existing CKB applications.
  • Documentation that can support further development of CKB privacy tooling.

12. Final Outcome

The final outcome will be an open-source Unlinked for CKB browser extension prototype demonstrating two complementary privacy features: experimental Tor-routed access to supported CKB RPC endpoints and local inspection of wallet-related information transmitted by dApps.

The project prioritizes functional software, reproducible demonstrations and practical developer deliverables.

The six-week grant will fund the development and testing needed to turn these ideas into a working prototype and establish a foundation for future improvements to extension browser privacy in the Nervos ecosystem.

item.title: Spark Program | MoniMkt: CKB Lending Validation Toolkit and Product Field Test
item.dc:creator: NOrththebear
item.description:
1. Project Overview

Project name: MoniMkt

One-line summary: A reusable CKB lending validation toolkit, field-tested with real users against the MoniMkt testnet product.

Positioning: The primary deliverable is a standalone, reusable validation toolkit for cell-based lending markets on CKB. MoniMkt is the first reference fixture and field test, not the product being funded. This directly follows the committee’s suggestion to focus on a testing suite or validation tool without broader market operations.

MoniMkt is the CKB equivalent of what Compound built for Ethereum: a pooled lending market where users supply, borrow, repay, and withdraw against collateral. The difference is that MoniMkt uses CKB cells directly. Market state, positions, vaults, and the oracle are cells, and the rules are enforced by CKB scripts.

The market and frontend already work on testnet. What is missing is a reusable way to validate lending behavior across CKB lending products, and real product evidence from users who are not the builder. This proposal delivers both, with the toolkit as the core and MoniMkt as the first field test.

2. Committee Alignment

This proposal is structured around the committee’s feedback:

  • The core deliverable is a standalone validation toolkit, not a market operations package.
  • MoniMkt is one reference fixture and field test, not the product being funded.
  • The work is testing and validation only.
  • There is no security hardening, no oracle operations, no mainnet work, no custody work, and no ongoing hosted beta.
  • The entire scope is one toolkit plus one bounded field test.

The product field test exists to prove the toolkit is useful in practice, not to turn Spark into an operations funder.

3. Team Profile

Applicant / core developer: North Bear, full-stack and Rust, protocol and smart-contract development.

  • GitHub: GitHub - NOrththebear/MoniMkt · GitHub
  • Email: capc55005@gmail.com
  • Discord: northbears

I built the MoniMkt contracts, testnet deployment, frontend, and oracle keeper. I also built Bees Network, a CKB observation-layer MVP deployed on Pudge testnet, including its cell-based registry, epoch accounting, and desktop client.

4. Product Background

CKB has strong custody and settlement primitives, but most users still meet CKB applications through wallets, forms, and transaction prompts that assume technical knowledge. A working contract is not the same as a usable product.

MoniMkt currently supports:

  • CKB wallet connection and account initialization.
  • Live reads of market and position cells.
  • RUSD supply and withdraw.
  • CKB collateral supply and withdraw.
  • RUSD borrow and repay.
  • Transaction lifecycle feedback.
  • Dashboard and activity views.
  • A multi-source CKB/USD oracle.

The product has been exercised end to end on testnet. What we do not have is:

  • A reusable validation harness that other CKB lending teams can use.
  • Evidence from users who are not the builder.
  • A clear answer to which product surfaces help or block real users.

5. What We Are Building

A. Core deliverable: CKB lending validation toolkit

A standalone, open-source toolkit for validating cell-based lending markets.

CLI and scenario format

  • A command-line runner that executes a lending scenario file.
  • A small scenario format for actors, actions, expected results, and failure cases.
  • Deterministic fixtures for market state, RUSD cells, CKB vaults, accounts, positions, and oracle cells.
  • One-command clean run against a local devnet or ckb-testtool.

Adapters

  • ckb-testtool adapter for script-level and transaction-level validation.
  • Local devnet adapter for end-to-end flows with real wallets and RPC.
  • A fixture builder that can target a new CKB lending market without rewriting the runner.

Scenario coverage

  • Supply and withdraw base asset.
  • Supply and withdraw collateral.
  • Borrow and repay.
  • Interest accrual and index updates.
  • Liquidation, absorb, and discounted collateral purchase.
  • Pause and approval behavior where supported.
  • Stale oracle, insufficient collateral, wrong witness, malformed cell data, wrong action, and capacity failures.
  • Token conservation and vault capacity checks.

Assertions and reports

  • Assertions on output cells, cell data, lock and type errors, token deltas, vault deltas, nonce changes, and transaction outcomes.
  • Deterministic pass or fail results.
  • JSON and HTML reports with scenario names, expected outcomes, actual outcomes, and transaction hashes.
  • CI templates so a project can run the suite on every push.

Documentation

  • A short integration guide for another CKB lending project.
  • A scenario authoring guide.
  • A “verify in five minutes” guide.
  • The MoniMkt fixture as a worked example.

B. MoniMkt field test

MoniMkt is the first reference fixture and the first real product test.

  • A fixed four-week validation round with 15 to 20 external CKB users.
  • Structured tasks covering connection, initialization, supply, borrow, repay, withdraw, and recovery from expected failures.
  • Wallet coverage across the CCC-supported wallets used by the product.
  • Short surveys, observed task completion, and follow-up interviews.
  • A weekly issue review during the test.

This is not a hosted beta operation. It is a bounded field test that produces evidence for the toolkit and for the product.

C. Product surface work needed for a fair test

The current frontend works, but it is still a builder’s interface. Before asking users to test the product, it needs a focused product surface pass:

  • A single frontend state model for wallet, account, market data, position, and transaction status.
  • A consistent transaction lifecycle: preparing, confirm in wallet, confirming, confirmed, rejected, and retry guidance.
  • Clearer wallet onboarding and recovery for JoyID, OKX Wallet, UTXO Global, and Khie.
  • Simpler supply, withdraw, borrow, and repay forms with validation and plain-language errors.
  • A dashboard that leads with the user’s position and next action.
  • Mobile layout, typography, and accessibility improvements.

This is not a feature expansion. It is the minimum product surface required to run a fair test and to demonstrate the toolkit against a real product.

D. Product fixes and report

  • Fix the highest-severity usability issues found during the field test.
  • Re-test the fixed flows with a subset of users.
  • Publish a prioritized product roadmap based on evidence.
  • Publish the toolkit’s scenario coverage, reports, and integration guide.

No contract changes. The MoniMkt market scripts and state model remain unchanged.

6. What This Proposal Does Not Fund

This is not a request for Spark to fund:

  • Smart contract development.
  • Security hardening or an external audit.
  • Oracle operations or keeper maintenance.
  • Mainnet deployment or custody work.
  • Hosted beta operations or ongoing support.
  • Tester incentives.
  • A token, a reward pool, or liquidity incentives.

The existing testnet infrastructure is sufficient. The grant covers the toolkit, the field test, and the minimum product surface needed for that test.

7. Execution Plan: 6 Weeks

Start on acceptance. The four-week field test begins after a two-week build phase.

Week 1: Toolkit foundation

Define the scenario format, CLI, fixtures, and assertion model. Build the ckb-testtool adapter and the first MoniMkt scenarios. Define the product test plan and hypotheses.

Milestone: a clean local run of the first scenario set.

Week 2: Toolkit coverage and beta build

Add devnet adapter, failure scenarios, JSON and HTML reports, CI template, and integration docs. Finish the product surface pass, onboarding, transaction states, and beta build. Prepare the test scripts and wallet matrix.

Milestone: public beta build and a documented toolkit that runs the MoniMkt fixture.

Weeks 3 to 6: Four-week field test

Run 15 to 20 testers through the structured tasks. Track task completion, wallet-specific issues, transaction outcomes, time to first supply, and qualitative feedback. Triage weekly, fix the highest-severity product issues, and re-test the fixes. Use the field test to refine the toolkit’s scenarios and reports.

Milestone: all testers have attempted the core flows; toolkit and product findings are recorded and prioritized.

Week 6 close-out

Publish the validation report, toolkit documentation, scenario pack, before-and-after product notes, a demo video, and the completion report.

Milestone: public toolkit release and product validation report.

8. Required Funding and Breakdown

Requested: USD 1,500, payable in CKB.

Why $1,500: This is one validation project with two coupled outputs. The reusable toolkit is the primary deliverable, and the four-week field test proves it against a real CKB lending product. A $1,000 budget would underfund either the toolkit or the field test.

Item Amount Use
Validation toolkit $600 CLI, scenario format, fixtures, ckb-testtool and devnet adapters, assertions, reports, CI, docs
Product surface for the field test $450 State model, transaction lifecycle, onboarding, forms, dashboard, mobile, accessibility
Field test design and facilitation $300 Test plan, task scripts, 15 to 20 testers, scheduling, interviews, weekly triage
Report, demo, and completion package $150 Analysis, public report, demo video, docs
Total $1,500

9. Deliverables and How to Verify

Deliverables

  1. Open-source CKB lending validation toolkit with CLI, scenario format, fixtures, adapters, assertions, and reports.
  2. A documented scenario pack with positive and negative lending cases.
  3. MoniMkt reference fixture and a five-minute integration guide.
  4. CI template and example report.
  5. Public beta build with the new product surface and transaction states.
  6. Product validation report with 15 to 20 testers, wallet coverage, task completion, transaction results, and verbatim feedback.
  7. Prioritized product roadmap.
  8. Demo video and completion report.

How to verify without code review

  • Run the toolkit’s published command against the MoniMkt fixture and inspect the pass/fail report.
  • Open the example JSON and HTML reports and confirm expected versus actual outcomes.
  • Read the scenario authoring and integration guides.
  • Open the public beta URL, connect a CKB wallet, and complete the core lending flow.
  • Compare the before-and-after product screenshots and notes.
  • Read the product validation report and check the measured results.
  • Open the provided testnet explorer links for the flows exercised during validation.
  • Watch the demo video.

10. Success Metrics

Toolkit metrics

Metric Target
Documented scenarios At least 15
Positive and negative cases At least 8 positive, 7 negative
One-command clean run Works on a clean checkout
Deterministic reports Same result on repeated runs
External integration guide One other CKB lending project can follow it without author help
CI template Passes on a sample repository

Product field-test metrics

Metric Target
External testers 15 to 20
Testers completing one full cycle At least 12
Wallet connection success At least 90% per tested wallet
Transaction success excluding deliberate failure tests At least 95%
Median time to first supply Under 5 minutes
Testers who can explain the next action from the dashboard At least 80%
Structured feedback responses At least 12
Critical usability blockers after fixes 0

The report will publish actual results, including misses and unresolved issues.

11. Current State vs Funded Work

Already built and live on testnet

  • MoniMkt market with RUSD base asset and CKB collateral.
  • 13 RISC-V scripts deployed with Type ID.
  • Working supply, withdraw, borrow, repay, collateral, absorb, and discounted collateral flows.
  • Static CKB frontend with CCC wallet connection and direct cell reads.
  • Multi-source CKB/USD oracle keeper.
  • 112 automated tests across contracts and integration scenarios.

Funded by this grant

  • Reusable validation toolkit and scenario pack.
  • MoniMkt field test with 15 to 20 users.
  • Product surface and frontend state work required for the test.
  • Product fixes, re-test, and a prioritized roadmap.
  • Public report, demo, and completion package.

Not claimed: this grant does not improve the protocol security model, oracle operations, mainnet readiness, or custody guarantees. Those remain separate work.

12. Risks and Limits

  • Toolkit scope. The toolkit must stay focused on lending scenarios and avoid becoming a general-purpose chain indexer or simulator.
  • Fixture assumptions. MoniMkt is the first fixture. The integration guide will state what another lending project must adapt.
  • Product surface only. This grant will not fix contract-level or oracle-level risks.
  • Wallet variance. CCC-supported wallets can behave differently. The field test records issues per wallet.
  • Small sample. 15 to 20 testers provide directional product evidence, not statistical proof.
  • Testnet conditions. Testnet CKB has no real value, and testers may need guidance on collateral amounts at current CKB prices.
  • No ongoing operations. The field test is a four-week window inside a six-week project, not a permanent hosted service.

13. CKB Alignment

MoniMkt is a native CKB product. The frontend reads live cells directly, uses CKB wallet signatures, and displays transaction outcomes from the cell model. It does not depend on an off-chain ledger or an account-based contract.

The validation toolkit is CKB-native as well. It exercises cell transitions, type and lock scripts, token conservation, vault capacity, and transaction-level failure behavior. It gives CKB lending teams a reusable way to validate their own markets rather than rebuilding test infrastructure from scratch.

14. Closing

The committee asked for a standalone testing suite or validation tool. This proposal makes that the core deliverable and uses MoniMkt as the first real fixture and field test.

The output is a reusable CKB lending validation toolkit, a documented scenario pack, a public product validation report, and a clear next-step roadmap. It does not fund market operations, security hardening, oracle maintenance, mainnet work, or an indefinite beta.

item.title: Spark Program | CapKey: Spend-Capped Sub-Key Covenants for Browser dApps and AI Agents
item.dc:creator: teeyml
item.description:
Project Name: CapKey
Applicant: Terry Jn. (TeeYml on GitHub)
Funding Requested: $720 (paid in CKB, payout address provided upon approval)
Duration: 5 Weeks
License: MIT
Contact: Nervos Talk direct message
Ecosystem Alignment: AI Machine Payments, Browser Self-Custody Sessions (BSS)

Applicant Profile

Terry Jn. (TeeYml on GitHub) is an independent full-stack and web3 engineer with experience building smart contracts, transaction serialization pipelines and developer tooling across UTXO and account-based ecosystems.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/TeeYml
  • Repository: https://github.com/TeeYml/capkey

1. Executive Summary

CapKey is an on-chain covenant vault protocol and client SDK for Nervos CKB that lets wallet holders delegate strictly bounded spending power to temporary sub-keys.

In modern Web3 applications and autonomous agent pipelines, key management faces a sharp tradeoff between user friction and catastrophic key exposure. In browser dApps, requiring a wallet popup for every 5 CKB micro-action creates unbearable user fatigue in games, streaming payments and social tipping. Conversely, handing an unconstrained hot private key to an AI agent or browser local storage exposes the entire wallet balance to theft from a single prompt injection or malicious dependency.

CapKey solves this natively at the CKB consensus level. By locking funds into a capkey-lock Vault Cell, the master account owner defines non-bypassable constraints:

  1. Per-Transaction Cap: A hard ceiling on how much can be spent in any individual transaction.
  2. Cumulative Allowance: An exact step-down budget across the lifetime of the sub-key.
  3. Single-Successor Rule: Exactly one vault Cell in and one out, so a spend cannot split or merge vaults to dodge the caps.
  4. Sequence Counter: Each delegate spend raises last_sequence by one, giving verifiers an ordered history.
  5. Owner Recovery: The owner can sweep or rotate the vault at any block.

Because CKB utilizes the UTXO Cell Model, these rules are enforced directly by recursive script covenants on the transaction outputs without requiring the heavy smart-contract account abstraction layers (ERC-4337) or centralized relayer infrastructure needed on account-based chains.

2. Motivation & Ecosystem Need

The Nervos Opportunity Map for AI, Machine Payments and Fiber in 2026 ( AI, machine payments, and Fiber in 2026: an opportunity map for CKB and Fiber developers ) designates Browser Self-Custody Sessions (BSS) as a high-priority track under “Validate Next”, highlighting two critical emerging use cases:

  • Enabling browser users to conduct repetitive on-chain interactions without signing continuous wallet popups.
  • Providing autonomous AI agents with scoped, bounded on-chain balances so they can pay for inference, data or tooling without access to the operator’s master treasury.

Why Existing Approaches Fall Short

Approach Architecture Failure Mode
Frequent Master Signing Cold wallet signs every micro-action Severe popup fatigue; breaks gameplay and real-time interaction flows
Hot Key In Local Storage / .env Unconstrained private key in app environment Full balance exposed; one XSS exploit or prompt injection drains all funds
Off-Chain Policy Linters (e.g. CellGuard) Off-chain client checks transaction JSON Stolen hot key bypasses the linter and broadcasts directly to CKB RPC nodes
Centralized Database Balances Custodial server tracks user credits Defeats self-custody; requires user trust and creates regulatory counterparty risk
EVM Account Abstraction (ERC-4337) Smart-contract wallet with session keys Extreme complexity; requires user-ops, bundlers, paymasters and high gas overhead

CapKey provides a native CKB answer: a lightweight, recursive covenant lock script where every sub-key spend is validated directly by CKB-VM nodes.

3. Protocol Architecture & Invariants

CapKey operates via a hierarchical key model: the Cold Master Key retains unconstrained ownership, while the Hot Delegate Key holds covenant-restricted spending permissions.

Vault Transition Flow

Input vault Cell (500 CKB, allowance 250, max_per_tx 100, seq 0)
  + input locked by delegate_lock_hash (its lock checks the signature)
        |
        v
Output 0: successor vault Cell (420 CKB, allowance 170, max_per_tx 100, seq 1)
Output 1: recipient Cell (79.99 CKB)
          80 CKB left the vault: 79.99 to the recipient and 0.01 as fee

Binary Cell Layout (CK01)

Lock Script Arguments (args) (64 bytes)

  • owner_lock_hash (32 bytes): lock hash of the owner wallet.
  • delegate_lock_hash (32 bytes): lock hash of the delegate key. Any CKB lock can fill this role.

Cell Data (28 bytes)

  • magic (4 bytes): ASCII identifier CK01.
  • max_per_tx (8 bytes, u64 LE): maximum shannons that may leave the vault in one transaction.
  • remaining_allowance (8 bytes, u64 LE): cumulative shannons the delegate may still spend.
  • last_sequence (8 bytes, u64 LE): counter raised by one on each delegate spend.

Design choice: the delegate’s own lock checks the signature

The delegate path requires an input in the same transaction locked by delegate_lock_hash. That lock verifies the signature over the whole transaction, so capkey-lock contains no signature code. This keeps the script at 27 KB and lets the delegate be secp256k1, a WebAuthn lock such as JoyID or any other lock already on CKB.

Consensus Rules

Owner path: an input locked by owner_lock_hash is present. The script accepts.

Delegate path: an input locked by delegate_lock_hash is present and all of these hold:

  1. One vault Cell is consumed and exactly one is created.
  2. Output 0 carries the same capkey-lock script and no type script.
  3. spent = input.capacity - output[0].capacity is above zero. It covers the recipient payment and the miner fee.
  4. spent <= max_per_tx.
  5. spent <= remaining_allowance.
  6. Output 0 data keeps max_per_tx, lowers remaining_allowance by exactly spent and raises last_sequence by one.

Known limits

  • CKB has no upper bound on when a transaction may be committed so a lock cannot enforce “valid until time T”. CapKey does not claim expiry. The allowance bounds the loss and the owner can sweep at any time.
  • Caps apply to capacity only. xUDT and Spore assets are out of scope.
  • The recipient is not restricted.

4. Current State & Proof of Execution

The core lock already exists and is public, written in Rust and tested in the real CKB-VM:

  • Script: contracts/capkey-lock, ckb-std 1.1, no_std, 27,712 bytes.
  • Tests: 12 ckb-testtool tests. Each rejection test asserts the exact script error code.
  • Measured: 38,085 cycles for a delegate spend and 22,648 for an owner sweep, with an always-success delegate lock in the harness.
  • Reproduce: make test

Existing vs Funded Scope

Component Status Today Funded Scope in Grant
capkey-lock script Done, 12 tests passing Hardening, review fixes and testnet deployment
Tests with a real signature lock Always-success locks only Tests against the secp256k1 lock and a WebAuthn lock, with real cycle numbers
@capkey/sdk None Transaction builders for create, delegate spend, chained spends and owner sweep
capkey CLI None issue, pay and verify against CKB RPC
Web app None Public testnet app with a non-extractable WebCrypto delegate key
Independent verifier None Standalone checker that validates a vault transition from RPC data alone

5. Milestone Roadmap & Deliverables

The funded work runs for 5 weeks in four milestones.

Milestone 1: Real signature locks and testnet deployment (Week 1)

  • Add tests where the delegate is the secp256k1 sighash lock and where it is a WebAuthn (P-256) lock. Publish the cycle cost of each.
  • Add the cases missing from the current suite: a delegate input present but spending a different vault, two vaults in one transaction and u64 boundary values.
  • Deploy capkey-lock to CKB testnet and publish the code hash and deployment transaction.
  • Deliverable: tag v0.2.0.

Milestone 2: TypeScript SDK and CLI (Weeks 2-3)

  • @capkey/sdk on CCC with builders for vault creation, delegate spend, chained unconfirmed spends (up to 3) and owner sweep.
  • capkey issue and capkey pay working against testnet.
  • Deliverable: published npm package and CLI.

Milestone 3: Public web app (Week 4)

  • Connect a testnet wallet, fund a vault and issue a delegate key.
  • The delegate key is a WebCrypto key with extractable: false stored in IndexedDB, so page scripts can sign but cannot export it.
  • A demo store spends from the vault with no wallet popups and shows remaining_allowance falling.
  • A “Simulate Rogue Drain” button submits an over-cap transaction and shows the node’s script error.
  • Deliverable: live URL.

Milestone 4: Verifier, guide and video (Week 5)

  • capkey verify <tx_hash> rebuilds the input state, outputs and caps from CKB RPC and prints pass or fail.
  • Integration guide for dApps and AI agent frameworks.
  • Short walkthrough video.
  • Deliverable: verifier, guide, video and a closing report.

6. How to Verify

Every milestone includes self-contained reproduction commands requiring no subjective review:

  1. Native Script Verification:

    git clone https://github.com/TeeYml/capkey.git
cd capkey
make test

    Every adversarial case fails inside the CKB script with its expected error code while valid transitions succeed.

  2. Public Web Experience:

    • Navigate to the hosted testnet web app.
    • Connect JoyID or MetaMask, deposit 500 CKB and issue a 100 CKB sub-key with a 25 CKB per-tx limit.
    • Click “Purchase Item (10 CKB)” three times: payments confirm on testnet with zero wallet popups.
    • Click “Simulate Rogue Drain (150 CKB)”: transaction is rejected by CKB RPC.
    • Click “Revoke & Sweep”: master key reclaims all remaining vault funds to the cold wallet.

  3. Independent RPC Verification:

    npx capkey verify <tx_hash> --rpc https://testnet.ckbapp.dev/

    Outputs parsed input vault parameters, deducted payment, fee breakdown, successor vault allowance and validation status.

  4. On-Chain Explorer Verification:

    • Inspect published transaction hashes on pudge.explorer.nervos.org proving live deployment, delegate spends and master revocations.

7. Budget Breakdown

The requested funding is $720, paid in CKB. Calculated bottom-up at $15/hour across 48 hours. The lock script and its first test suite are already written and are not billed.

Milestone / Deliverable Hours Cost (USD)
Milestone 1: Real signature lock tests, extra cases and testnet deployment 10 $150
Milestone 2: @capkey/sdk builders, chained spends and CLI 16 $240
Milestone 3: Public web app with WebCrypto delegate and attack simulator 14 $210
Milestone 4: Independent verifier, guide and video 8 $120
Total 48 $720

Disbursement will follow the committee’s standard milestone schedule. Payout address will be provided upon approval when requested.

8. Post-Grant Maintenance Plan

Following the completion of the 5-week grant scope, I commit to:

  • 6 months of active maintenance for the @capkey/sdk repository.
  • Responding to community issues and pull requests on GitHub within 48 hours.
  • Ensuring ongoing compatibility with updates to CCC, ckb-std and CKB node releases.
  • Providing technical guidance to any ecosystem dApp or AI agent team seeking to integrate CapKey sub-keys.

item.title: Spark Program | CKB Script Bench: How Well Do AI Models Write CKB Scripts?
item.dc:creator: Shobiye_Abdulazeem
item.description:
1. Project Overview

Project name: CKB Script Bench

One-sentence summary: An open, re-runnable test set of 24 CKB on-chain script tasks that measures whether AI-written lock and type scripts compile against the current ckb-std and hold up against malicious transactions, and whether CKB’s official AI resources fix the failures. A pilot on 3 tasks already found that the main failure is outdated or invented API use, not unsafe logic.

Project type: open-source benchmark (task set + hidden security tests + runner) and a public report, run in ckb-testtool / ckb-debugger. No chain deployment needed.

Funding requested: $980, paid in CKB

Duration: 6 weeks

CKB Script Bench is a measurement, not another AI assistant. It does not build a chatbot, a scaffold or an MCP server. It tests the ones that already exist and publishes where AI-written CKB scripts break.

2. Team Profile

Shobiye Abdulazeem (solo), backend / smart-contract engineer, Lagos, Nigeria].

  • I built Stellar tags, Human-readable payment tags for the Stellar network. Send to alice*stellartags instead of a 56-character G... address.
  • Has shipped on Stellar/Soroban.
  • Anything that breaks in ckb-testtool, ckb-debugger or the official docs gets written up and filed upstream.

GitHub: github.com/Abdulazeem-code · Repo: github.com/Abdulazeem-code/ckb-script-bench · Contact: Nervos Talk DM

3. Project Background

Why I want to build this. AI written ckb script was good, But it doesn’t seem safe for the developer and whatever product is being worked on And also Not all its code compile against the current ckb-std.

The gap this targets. CKB now officially recommends AI agents for script work. The docs publish llms.txt and llms-full.txt, list a community MCP server (CKB AI) and an agent skill (CKB Dev Skills), and ship a starter prompt to “Write, Test, and Deploy a CKB Script”. Nobody has published numbers on whether the scripts these agents write are safe.

An AI-written CKB script can fail in two ways. It may not compile against the current ckb-std, because the model learned an older API or invents methods. Or it compiles but is too permissive: a lock that ignores the script group, a token that doesn’t check overflow, or a timelock that reads since wrongly. The second is the expensive failure, so every task carries attack tests. The pilot below found the first is the common one today, and it is the one the official AI resources should fix.

Existing work, and what this reuses.

Existing What it covers How this project relates
ckb-ai-bench Whether the CKB AI MCP server improves a coding agent; 7 tasks verified by direct CKB RPC on devnet/testnet; no published run yet Complementary. It measures tool help on chain operations; this measures script correctness under attack. The CKB AI MCP condition is left out here so the two do not test the same thing. Tasks and tests are published openly, so ckb-ai-bench or anyone else can reuse them
Official AI resources (AGENTS.md in ckb-script-templates, llms-full.txt, CKB Dev Skills) What agents should read and how they should work These are the conditions being tested, used unmodified
ckb-testtool + ckb-debugger Running scripts against crafted transactions The test engine. No new runtime is built
Nervos Brain (Spark, completed) Answering developer questions Different question: answers vs. code that holds up

What is new: compile checks against the current ckb-std plus hidden attack tests, run on agent-written scripts from a developer-style brief, with each official AI resource switched on and off, published so anyone can re-check every number.

Pilot evidence (already done, not funded). Three tasks were built and given to ChatGPT and Gemini in fresh chats, with no follow-up messages. Each answer was compiled unedited and run against the task’s positive and attack tests.

Run Model Task Prompt Result
01 ChatGPT A01 hash-preimage lock full spec Correct: 3/3 valid, 6/6 attacks rejected
01 Gemini A02 absolute timelock full spec Correct: 3/3, 7/7
01 ChatGPT (free) A01 hash-preimage lock brief Correct: 3/3, 6/6
01 Gemini Pro A02 absolute timelock brief Correct: 3/3, 7/7
01 ChatGPT (free) B01 simple token brief Compile error: calls Script::hash(), which doesn’t exist. Correct after a minimal fix
01 Gemini Pro B01 simple token brief Compile error: SysError match written for an older ckb-std. Correct after a one-line fix
02 ChatGPT (free) B01 simple token brief + AGENTS.md Correct: 4/4, 7/7
02 Gemini Pro B01 simple token brief + AGENTS.md Compile error: the same SysError match. Correct after the same fix

None of the 8 answers was unsafe; every failure was API knowledge. 3 of the 4 answers to the Tier B brief failed to compile against ckb-std 1.1. Adding the official AGENTS.md fixed one of the two: it steered ChatGPT to real high_level functions, but it says nothing about what changed between ckb-std versions, so Gemini repeated its mistake.

This is one answer per model per condition: a signal, not a measurement. Prompts, unedited answers, compiler output and results are in the repo (run 01, run 02). The funded run repeats every cell with more tasks, models and runs.

4. Solution

What anyone gets (from week 5):

  1. Clone the repo and run one command. It re-runs every hidden test against the published agent outputs, with no API keys needed.
  2. Open the results page: pass rates per task, per model, per condition, and every unsafe script with the attack that broke it.
  3. Optionally plug in your own model or agent setup and score it on the same 24 tasks.

The task set (24 tasks, Rust + ckb-std, as the official agent instructions recommend):

Tier Tasks Examples
A. Lock scripts 6 (2 built) hash-preimage lock, owner lock by lock hash, absolute and relative timelocks via since, 2-of-3 multisig-lite
B. Type scripts 9 (1 built) counter that only increments, simple token (output sum ≤ input sum unless owner mints), immutable data cell, one-time-unique cell (Type ID style)
C. Combined 9 escrow with refund after deadline, vault that must keep capacity, lock + type pairing, script reading cell deps

Each task has a plain-English spec (what an agent sees), 2–4 positive tests and 4–8 hidden attack tests (what it never sees). The attacks are the common CKB mistakes: extra inputs in the same script group, unchecked args length, outputs created without the type script, wrong since flags, sums checked on one side only.

Each task also has a brief: the interface only (args, cell data and witness format), the way a developer would ask. Scored runs use the brief, because in the pilot the full spec turned the safety rules into a checklist that every model followed. The set leans toward Tiers B and C because every Tier A answer in the pilot was correct; Tier A stays as a floor.

Conditions, each with the same prompt and the same three models (chosen at kickoff: two leading closed models and one open-weight model):

  • C0 bare model, no CKB context
  • C1 + AGENTS.md from ckb-script-templates (the pilot’s condition)
  • C2 + official llms-full.txt
  • C3 + CKB Dev Skills agent skill

The MCP server condition is left to ckb-ai-bench so the two projects do not overlap.

Pre-registered hypotheses. Posted on this thread before week 1. Anyone may propose an extra attack test, and I commit to adding it before the scored run.

# Hypothesis Pass if If it fails, the report publishes
H1 Bare models often write CKB scripts that don’t compile against the current ckb-std In C0, ≥ 30% of first attempts on Tier B and C tasks fail to compile The real first-try compile rate, and the API errors behind each failure
H2 Bare models rarely write unsafe scripts In C0, < 10% of scripts that pass all positive tests fail an attack test Every unsafe script with the attack that broke it
H3 Official AI context cuts compile failures The best of C1–C3 cuts first-try compile failures by ≥ 15 points vs C0 Per-resource deltas, including tasks where context made it worse
H4 A one-page “ckb-std 1.x changes and common mistakes” note, written from scored-run failures, fixes the top errors On 6 held-out tasks, adding the note to C1 raises first-try compile by ≥ 10 points The note anyway, marked as not shown to help

What this does not claim. 24 tasks and three models are a sample, not a ranking of AI vendors. The report states run counts and variance and makes no claim beyond them.

5. Technical Architecture

Task layout (as already in the repo): tasks/<id>/spec.md (full spec), tasks/<id>/brief.md (what the model sees in scored runs), contracts/<name>/ (reference solution, from ckb-script-templates) and tests/src/<name>.rs (positive p* and attack a* tests). The 3 pilot tasks are public. Attack tests for the other 21 stay in a private branch until the scored run is frozen, then are published.

Runner (extends the working scripts/render_prompt.sh and scripts/run_candidate.sh):

  1. Builds the prompt: spec + template + the condition’s context (none / AGENTS.md / llms-full.txt / CKB Dev Skills).
  2. Calls the model once, then allows up to 3 repair turns that show only compiler errors. No web access, no test results shown. This keeps runs cheap and comparable.
  3. Builds the script to RISC-V in a throwaway copy of the repo inside a pinned Docker image, then runs positive and attack tests with ckb-testtool, which executes through the CKB-VM the same way ckb-debugger does.
  4. Writes one JSON line per run: task, model, condition, run number, compiled yes/no, positives passed, attacks passed, cycles used, tokens, cost, and the generated source.

Scoring:

  • Compiles first try → the unedited answer builds without errors
  • Compiles after repair → builds within 3 repair turns that show only compiler errors
  • Happy-path pass → all positive tests pass
  • Full pass → all positive and all attack tests pass
  • Unsafe → happy-path pass but ≥ 1 attack accepted

Run size: 24 tasks × 4 conditions × 3 models × 2 runs = 576 runs, plus 36 runs for H4 (6 held-out tasks × 3 models × 2 runs). Each run is about 10–20k tokens. Two runs per cell, instead of three, keeps the added AGENTS.md condition inside the same API budget.

H4 hold-out: 6 of the 21 private tasks are frozen as held-out before the scored run. The note is written only from failures on the other 15, then tested on the 6.

Verification without API keys: all generated sources are committed. make verify rebuilds every script and re-runs every test from the committed sources, and make report rebuilds every number in the report from the JSON logs.

Hard parts, which are the point of the test:

  • Fair attack tests: each one follows from a rule the brief states (“only the owner can mint” covers the overflow and owner-on-output attacks), and the full spec spells it out.
  • Telling API errors from logic errors: every answer is scored unedited, then again after compile-only repair turns, so a script that fails to compile still gets a safety verdict.
  • Model outputs vary run to run; two runs per cell and published variance handle this.
  • Cycle limits: a script that is correct but exceeds a sane cycle budget is reported separately, not counted as safe.

Out of scope: mainnet or testnet deployment, building a new AI assistant or MCP server, fine-tuning models, C and JS scripts (possible follow-up).

6. Weekly Execution Plan

Week Focus Concrete output
0 (before start) Post hypotheses and the 24 task titles on this thread Hypotheses and task titles posted and locked
1 Automated runner (model API calls, 4 conditions, repair turns), pinned Docker image, scoring; the remaining 4 Tier A tasks make verify passes on reference solutions for all 6 Tier A tasks and B01; tag v0.1
2 The remaining 17 Tier B and C tasks; reference solution and broken copies for every task All 24 reference solutions pass every test and every broken copy is caught; community attack-test proposals merged
3 Automated pilot run (1 model, C0, 1 run) to find unfair tests; freeze the 6 hold-out tasks Pilot results posted on this thread; any test changed is listed with the reason; attack tests frozen by commit hash
4 Scored run: 576 runs; write the note from the 15 non-held-out private tasks; 36 H4 runs Raw JSON logs and all generated sources committed
5 Results page and report draft; publish attack tests Results page live; report draft posted for comments
6 Final report, CKB script mistakes note, upstream issues Report and note published; issues filed for any docs or tool gaps found; closing post on this thread

7. Funding Requirements: $980 in CKB

Bottom-up at $15/hour, 54 hours, plus model API costs.

Item Hours Cost (USD)
Runner, pinned Docker image, scoring, make verify / make report 10 150
Tier A: 4 remaining lock-script tasks (2 already built, not funded), reference solutions, positive + attack tests 4 60
Tiers B and C: 17 remaining tasks (1 already built, not funded), reference solutions, positive + attack tests 22 330
Pilot run and fixing unfair tests 4 60
Scored run supervision and the mistakes note 5 75
Results page and report 7 105
Upstream issues and closing post 2 30
Model API usage, ~610 runs at 10–20k tokens each (estimate; invoices published, any unused amount reported) – 170
Total 54 980

20% at launch ($196). The remaining 80% ($784) on completion against the deliverables in section 8. Fund usage is disclosed at completion against this table.

8. Deliverables and Verification

None of these checks needs a code review or an API key.

Deliverable How to verify
Task set (24 tasks) Clone the repo, run make verify-reference: every reference solution passes every positive and attack test
Attack tests are real Run make verify-broken: each task ships 1–2 deliberately wrong solutions, and the attack tests catch every one
Scored results Run make verify: rebuilds all ~610 committed agent-written scripts and re-runs every test; results match the published logs
Report numbers (H1–H4) Run make report on the published JSON logs; diff against the published report
Tests were frozen before scoring The attack-test commit hash posted on this thread in week 3 predates the scored-run logs
Results page Open the link from this thread: filter by task, model and condition; each unsafe script links to its source and the attack that broke it
CKB script mistakes note One page in the repo; H4 result shows whether it helped on the 6 held-out tasks
Upstream notes UPSTREAM.md lists each docs or tooling gap found, each linked to an issue in the relevant repo

9. Current State vs. Funded Scope

Already exists (not funded): a public repo, ckb-script-bench, with 3 finished tasks (A01 hash-preimage lock, A02 absolute timelock, B01 simple token). Each has a full spec, a brief, a reference solution, and positive and attack tests: 30 tests, all passing. Every attack test was checked against a deliberately broken copy of the reference with the bug it targets, and all 12 broken copies are caught by exactly that test. Scripts render the prompts and score any model’s answer (CORRECT / WORKS BUT UNSAFE / BROKEN / COMPILE ERROR). Two pilot runs produced 8 model answers (section 3).

Funded by this grant: the remaining 21 tasks and tests, the automated runner (model API calls, repair turns) and Docker image, the automated pilot and scored runs, results page, report, the ckb-std changes note, upstream issues.

Explicitly out of scope: deployment to any network, a new AI assistant or MCP server, model fine-tuning, C or JS scripts, ranking AI vendors.

10. CKB Ecosystem Alignment

  • AI-assisted developer onboarding, one of Spark’s three stated directions, approached as measurement: it tests the AI resources CKB already recommends instead of building another one.
  • Problem before solution: the pilot already tested the original idea. Unsafe scripts didn’t appear in 8 answers; compile failures against the current ckb-std did, in 3 of 4 Tier B answers. The hypotheses follow that evidence, and H2 says plainly that unsafe scripts may be rare.
  • Anyone can verify it: every number rebuilds from committed sources and logs with one command and no API keys.
  • Reuses before building: ckb-testtool, ckb-debugger, ckb-script-templates, the official llms-full.txt and CKB Dev Skills, all unmodified; tasks published openly for reuse by ckb-ai-bench or anyone else.
  • Useful after the grant: DevRel and tool authors (CKB AI, CKB Dev Skills, docs) can re-run the bench after each change to see whether scripts compile and hold up better. The pilot already found one gap to report: AGENTS.md says nothing about what changed in ckb-std 1.x.
  • Honest limit: a sample of 24 tasks, three models and Rust only. It shows where agents fail on CKB, not which AI is best.

Risks and Mitigations

Risk Mitigation
Overlap with ckb-ai-bench Scope split stated up front: they cover MCP help on chain operations, this covers script safety, and the MCP condition is left out here. Tasks published openly for reuse
Attack tests are unfair or too strict Every attack maps to a sentence in the spec; week-3 pilot finds unfair tests; changes listed publicly before tests are frozen
Tasks leak into future model training The 3 pilot tasks are public and reported separately; attack tests for the other 21 stay private until the scored run is frozen; 6 held-out tasks; the runner accepts new task versions
API costs exceed estimate Repair turns capped at 3; run count fixed in advance; if short, drop the open-weight model’s second run first and say so in the report
Models update mid-run Exact model versions and dates recorded per run; whole scored run done inside week 4

item.title: CKB Pulse today: a new look, lessons from real fixes, and CKB inside your tools
item.dc:creator: LusoCryptoLabs
item.description:
CKB Pulse started six weeks ago as one page that shows who is building on CKB, live. It has grown into something larger: a place where the work of every CKB builder is seen, credited, and turned into lessons the next builder can use. This post is what it does today.

VIDEO: Luso Crypto Labs on X: "Who's building on CKB right now? CKB Pulse shows it, live. And every fix a builder ships becomes a lesson for the next one: 198 so far, each linked to its commit. In your AI agent and on your pull requests. Free and open source. https://t.co/ICccqV4x2Q" / X

CKB Pulse

CKB Pulse

Pulse shows the public work of the CKB ecosystem as it happens, from GitHub: projects, people and updates in one place.

In short

  • Live. Every push, pull request, review, issue and release in the CKB projects on GitHub, as it happens. In the 30 days to 19 November: 5,514 updates by 213 people in 209 projects, not counting our own. Bots and AI agents are left out.
  • A new look. The whole site was redesigned, in dark and light, with a first page that says what it is.
  • Lessons from real fixes. 198 lessons so far, drawn from the public commits of 47 CKB projects. Each one is checked against the commit it came from and links to it.
  • Credit where the work was done. Every project has a card with who works on it and what CKB learned from it. Maintainers can confirm the lessons from their own project.
  • Inside your tools. An MCP server for AI agents, a check of your code against the lessons, and a GitHub Action that brings the lessons to your pull requests.
  • Free and open source (MIT), in English, 中文 and Português, on a phone or a computer.

A new look

The site was redesigned from top to bottom: straight corners, strong type, one red signal, and the name of who makes it under the title. The reading pages follow your device in dark or light, and you can switch. First-time visitors land on a page that says what Pulse is before the live view opens.

The address changed too: pulse.lusocryptolabs.com. Old links keep working.

What the ecosystem learned, kept for the next builder

Most of what builders learn on CKB stays in a commit message, or in nobody’s notes. Someone finds out that an absolute epoch since needs its flag, or that completeFeeBy adds a change output where they expected an output to shrink, fixes it, and moves on. The next builder hits the same wall.

Pulse reads the public commits of the projects it follows and keeps what they teach as short lessons: the rule, why it matters, the code before and after when the commit shows it, and the commit itself. A lesson is released only after it is checked against that commit and against the project’s code as it is today. A lesson that stops being true comes down.

  • Browse and learn: CKB Pulse · What CKB learned, by topic and by level, with a start page, a glossary and a review mode.
  • Credit: every lesson names the project and links the commit. Every project card lists “What CKB learned from this project”.
  • Confirmed by maintainers: if you own a project, wrote the commit, or are a public member of its organisation, you can confirm or correct its lessons from the lesson page, one by one or all at once. A confirmed lesson shows your name. The first 21 are confirmed, all from our own repositories. Yours are next, if you want them to be.
  • Open data: all of it as JSON, under CC BY 4.0: https://pulse.lusocryptolabs.com/learned.json

The lessons come to you

Reading a list of lessons is one way. Having them arrive while you work is better.

In your AI agent (click for more details) On every pull request (click for more details)

Who builds on what

Which CKB libraries do projects really use? Pulse reads the dependency files of every project it follows. The list is made by use: a library appears when several builders use it, and leaves by itself when nobody builds on it any more.

Today: CCC in 124 projects, ckb-std in 89, ckb-testtool in 77, Molecule in 36, and nine more. If you maintain a library, this is your reach, updated twice a day: CKB Pulse · Who builds on what · CCC

Also there

  • Digests for the day, the week and the month: the busiest projects and people, and what shipped. CKB Pulse · Last 7 days
  • Follow projects and people on your device, and share what they ship.
  • A badge for your README, and a feed.
  • An API for everything on the page: CKB Pulse · What you can do with CKB Pulse

Limits

  • GitHub only. On-chain activity, private repositories and work outside GitHub do not show.
  • Projects are found automatically, by the CKB libraries they use and by how they describe themselves. A check today found about 60 active projects Pulse was missing, and most are followed now. Some are surely still missing: suggest yours on the page.
  • A lesson comes from one project’s commit unless it says otherwise. Read the source before you rely on one.
  • If you want your project or your account out of Pulse, open an issue and it is done: Issues · LusoCryptoLabs/ckb-pulse · GitHub

Questions for you

  • What should Pulse answer that it does not today?
  • If you maintain a project with lessons on Pulse: are they right? Your confirmation, or your correction, makes them worth more to everyone.
  • Would you put the action on your repository? What would stop you?
What would you use most?
What would you use most?
  • Following projects and people live
  • The daily, weekly and monthly digests
  • The lessons from real fixes
  • Pulse inside my AI agent (MCP)
  • The lessons on my pull requests (GitHub Action)

item.title: CKB Mixer(混币器)——Tornado Cash on CKb
item.dc:creator: tianlitao
item.description:
过去一段时间用AI做了一个小项目，现在整条链路已经在 CKB 公共测试网上跑通了，发出来给有兴趣的人看。

一句话：用 Groth16 + Poseidon Merkle 树在 CKB 上实现了「存款 → 零知识证明 → 匿名取款」，所有验证逻辑写在真实的 CKB-VM 脚本里，能上链、能取钱；另外做了一个存款意向 + 聚合者的 v2，以及一个浏览器里就能用的网页 demo。

  • 代码：https://github.com/tianlitao/ckb-mixer
  • 线上 demo（仅测试网）：https://ckb-mixer.nervosscan.com/

为什么这件事在 CKB 上值得单独做一遍

Tornado Cash 在 EVM 上靠合约存储「这张 commitment 已经用过了」，CKB 的 cell 模型没有便宜的链上 map。但反过来，CKB 给了两个在 EVM 上不可能的结构性好处：

  1. 链上不需要存 Merkle 树。 池子 cell 里只有 1,640 字节状态：30 个历史根、20 层 frontier、nullifier 集合的根。树由脚本按 frontier 增量维护，存款时约 20 次 Poseidon。
  2. 取款交易不需要任何签名。 收款地址和手续费被电路绑进证明，交易只有 1 个输入（池子 cell）、2 个输出。没有中继者也能上链，也没人能把收款人换成自己——这一点在 EVM 上必须靠 relayer 合约配合才成立。

代价也很 CKB：所有池子共用一个 cell，任何存款/取款都得花它。Tornado 的每笔交易独立、可并行；这里是个单点。这正是 v2 要解决的问题（通过聚合器和意图cell）。

一、它怎么工作

一个池子就是一个 cell：

部分 内容
type 池子脚本，args = 面额 ‖ 验证密钥 cell 的 data hash ‖ 池子 lock 的 code hash / hash type
lock 池子 lock，逻辑是「这个 cell 必须带池子 type script」——没有私钥，谁也没法把池子锁死
data 1,640 字节池子状态：next_index ‖ root_pos ‖ 30 个历史根 ‖ 20 层 frontier ‖ nullifier 集合根
  • 存款：commitment 写在 witness 里，脚本用 frontier 把它追加进 depth-20 的 Poseidon 树，并要求输出 cell 的 data 逐字节等于新状态、capacity 恰好 输入 + 面额。一笔交易只记录一个新根，所以证明在之后 30 笔存款交易内都有效。
  • 取款：脚本依次检查根在历史里 → 收款 cell 必须是池子之后的那个输出、无 type 无 data、capacity 恰好 面额 − fee → 把 nullifierHash 插进 256 层稀疏 Merkle 树（要求「插入前」的根等于当前集合根）→ 用链上的验证密钥 cell 验证 Groth16。
  • 电路（5,322 约束，4 个公开输入）：commitment = Poseidon(nullifier, secret)，nullifierHash = Poseidon(nullifier, index)。nullifier 绑定了叶子下标，所以同一个 commitment 存两次会有两个不同的 nullifierHash、两笔都能取——链上没有「commitment 已用」表也能防重复花。
  • nullifier 集合用自研的 256 层 SMT：每层一次 blake2b，证明是 32 字节 bitmap + 非空兄弟。取款时约 1.96M cycles。

二、一次取款要多少 cycles

默认构建（opt-level 3），本地 ckb-testtool，多次运行波动 < 0.2%：

阶段 cycles 占比
Groth16 验证 约 67.4M 97%
nullifier 集合（256 层 blake2b） 约 1.96M 2.8%
VM 启动 + 加载 276 KB 脚本 70,722 0.1%
读状态 / 收款检查 / 输出比对 约 86k 0.1%
合计 约 69.4M–69.5M 单块上限的 2%

存款约 8.4M（0.24%），其中 8.25M 是 20 次 Poseidon。批量存款每多一笔约 +0.4M。

编译档位的取舍很值得一说。opt-level = z 把二进制缩小 2.3 倍，但 cycles 反而多 47%：

变体 pool-type 体积 部署锁仓 存款 ×1 取款
default（opt 3） 276,640 B 27.7 万 CKB 8.40M 69.4M
size（opt z） 121,400 B 12.1 万 CKB 11.26M 102.3M
bext（opt 3 + 位扩展指令） 269,936 B 27.0 万 CKB 8.31M 68.6M

1 字节占 1 CKB，部署一次所有池子共用；但 size 档每笔取款要多花约 3300 万 cycles，并且越过节点默认的 max_tx_verify_cycles = 70M（默认档的 69.4M 也只比它低不到 1%，电路一改就可能越界）。

三、测试网上实测

2026-11-17 与 11-18 在 ckb_testnet（公共节点 testnet.ckb.dev）上跑了两轮。上链的是 size 构建（水龙头每个地址只给 30 万 CKB，default 构建光部署就要 29.7 万）：

项目 结果
部署（验证密钥 + 两个脚本） 141,614 字节，14.1 万 CKB 永久锁定
建池 面额 100 CKB，池子 cell 永久占 1,819 CKB
v1 跑完 5 笔存款 / 5 笔取款，取款约 1.025 亿 cycles，12–23 秒出块
超过 70M 能不能上链 能。 五笔 1.025 亿的取款交给公共节点后都正常打包
链上 vs 本地 cycles 相差 0.2%–0.5%
同块连发 一笔存款 + 两笔取款首尾相接（每笔花前一笔尚未上链的输出），三笔进了同一个块
对抗性 dry-run 重放、改收款人、抬 fee、少付、直接花池子、付一份钱存两个 commitment……6 种全部被拒，退出码符合预期

链上历史还能完整重放：工具每次运行都从建池交易沿池子 cell 的血缘读回全部交易，用同一个 mixer-core 重新执行，得到的 1,640 字节状态和 capacity 与链上 cell 逐字节一致，否则不往下做。

四、v2：把存款人的签名和池子 cell 解耦

v1 最大的现实问题是：存款人的 sighash 签名覆盖了「花的是哪一个池子 cell」，前面插进一笔交易，这笔存款就得重签。v2 做了三处改动：

改动 解决什么
存款意向 cell：用户把「面额 + 小费」锁进一个带 commitment 的 cell，不碰池子 存款不再和任何人抢 cell，签一次名就结束
批量 action：一笔池子交易处理任意多个意向 + 任意多笔取款 一次花池子 cell 办完很多人的事
池子 Type ID 意向 cell 必须能唯一指名「哪个池子」

取款本来就没有签名，证明只绑定 root、收款人、fee——所以一笔取款天然就是一条链下消息，谁拿到都能装进自己构造的交易里。于是多了一个不需要许可、不需要押金的角色：聚合者。它收集链上意向和链下取款消息，拼成批次，赚小费和 fee；偷不了钱、改不了收款人，最坏只是不干活。

flowchart LR
  A[用户 A 签名] --> IA[意向 cell A]
  B[用户 B 签名] --> IB[意向 cell B]
  C[用户 C：链下取款消息] --> AG
  D[用户 D：链下取款消息] --> AG
  IA --> AG[聚合者拼批次]
  IB --> AG
  AG --> P[池子 cell 新状态]
  AG --> RC[收款 cell C]
  AG --> RD[收款 cell D]

v2 同样在测试网上跑过（2026-11-18，55 笔存款、55 笔取款，size 构建）：

批次 链上 cycles 占块上限 出块
8 笔取款 8.23 亿 23.5% 15 s
16 笔取款 16.42 亿 46.9% 24 s
20 笔取款 20.54 亿 58.7% 14 s
  • 大交易和小交易一样在十几到二十几秒内出块；本地测得上限是 50 笔（默认构建）/ 34 笔（size），受限于资金，链上只试到 20 笔。
  • 手续费按权重收，不按字节：max(字节数, cycles × 597,000 / 3.5G)。20 笔取款的交易只有 13.6 KB，权重约 350 KB，按 5,000 shannons/KB 付 0.0175 CKB——聚合者从 20 笔里收 0.2 CKB，依然划算。
  • 撤回受共识保护：意向建好立刻撤回，节点回 Immature；过了 6 个块同一笔交易上链。
  • 两个聚合者抢同一批意向（真的发出去）：先到的批次手续费 13,315 shannons，对手出 13,315、15,978 都被拒（expect it to >= 17309），出 18,641 后被接受并上链，先到的被标 RBFRejected。规则与节点源码一致。

五、网页 demo

在 v2 之上做了一个纯静态页面 + 一个 Cloudflare Worker 聚合者：

  • 页面：https://ckb-mixer.nervosscan.com/（中 / 英双语）
  • 用 CCC 官方的 <ccc-connector> 连钱包；存款签一次名就留下「回执」；取款证明在浏览器里生成（约 1 秒），消息交给聚合者，或者点「自己发送（保底）」（不需要签名、不需要事先有 CKB）。
  • 页面和聚合者都从建池交易起重放池子全部交易，与链上 cell 逐字节比对；票据的两张随机数只存在浏览器 localStorage 里。
  • 聚合者每分钟一次 cron，把等着的意向和收到的取款拼成批次；GET /info 能看到它的地址和参数。

截至 2026-11-19：池子 2,250 CKB，61 笔存款、59 笔取款、2 笔未取，重放结果与链上 cell 一致。线上 cron 已经真的打包过带取款的批次。

  • Website: umojaverse.xyz

  • LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/umojaversepeeps/posts/?viewAsMember=true

  • Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/umojaversepeeps/

Summary

Umojaverse is an Africa-focused builder community that brings blockchain, web3 and general tech together from the grassroots and across borders, so people learn and build products of real value. Through campus tours, ideathons, workshops and hackerhouses, it takes people from first curiosity to working prototypes.

The CKB Productathon is a competitive programme in Kenya that turns builders into teams with live products on CKB mainnet. It runs in two parts. The first is virtual: expert-led training on CKB technology and on building a startup, while teams ship and gather real users. The second is a two-day physical hackerhouse on the shore of Lake Victoria, where teams that have gone live build, demo and pitch for prizes. Teams with a working product and teams with a new idea and a credible execution plan can both apply, and the aim is the same: products that ship, win user validation and keep growing.

  • Ask: $10,925 for the full programme, from planning to follow-up.

  • Timeline (tentative): planning in December 2026, programme from January to early February 2027, follow-up support until mid-March 2027.

  • Teams: up to 15 teams of three at the hackerhouse.

  • The rule: only teams live on CKB mainnet can enter the hackerhouse, and to win a prize a team must show on-chain activity from at least 5 beta users.

Why this is needed, why Umojaverse, why now

Why it is needed. Kenya has talented builders and no shortage of events, but too few of them ship products that real users depend on. Workshops and ideathons tend to end at the idea or the demo, and the hard part that follows has little support: deploying to mainnet, finding the first users and keeping the product running.

Three gaps hold builders back. There is no structured path from a first contract to a mainnet product. Mentors who have shipped and found users are scarce and hard to reach outside the big cities. And builders work alone, without a room of peers building beside them to share fixes, pressure and momentum.

CKB makes this gap worth closing. Its cell model, RISC-V based virtual machine and flexible scripts let builders create their own product logic, not just move tokens, but that flexibility is hard to learn alone. Guided, hands-on training turns it into an advantage, and every product that goes live on mainnet with real users is lasting proof of adoption for the ecosystem. Making live mainnet use the measure of success changes the incentive: builders are rewarded for shipping and getting users, not for attending.

Why Umojaverse. Umojaverse is a builder community, not a one-off event organiser, and this programme is the next step of work we already do. We take builders from first curiosity to working prototypes through campus tours, ideathons, workshops and hackerhouses, in person across Kenya and, through the Pulse East Africa HackFest, in five African countries. That gives this programme five things it needs:

  • Reach. An established builder community and presence across Kenya and wider Africa, so the open call draws serious applicants.

  • Proven delivery. Experience running multi-day, in-person hackerhouses and multi-country events, from venues and logistics to mentors, judging and content.

  • Teaching depth. A lead organiser who is a blockchain educator and developer, backed by a network of seasoned builders to teach, mentor and judge.

  • A CKB footing. We are already introducing Kenyan builders to CKB, and we know the questions they ask and where they get stuck.

  • Follow-through. We stay with builders after the event, through follow-up support and public recordings that keep teaching long after the programme ends.

This means we can run the programme end to end: recruit the teams, teach them, bring them together, showcase them and keep supporting them.

Why now. Three things line up. First, the tools are ready: builder tooling such as CCC and OffCKB makes it practical to go from a first script to a mainnet deployment inside a short programme. Second, builder attention in Kenya is warm and will cool without a concrete next step. Recent CKB activity needs a destination with a deadline, prizes and a place to build. Third, the calendar works: planning in December and a January start use the weeks after the holidays, and teams that ship to mainnet by early February get months of real use to prove adoption before mid-year. A month of follow-up support then turns a weekend of building into traction.

Previous work

Umojaverse has run builder programmes across Kenya, from first workshops to hackerhouses. Five pieces of work matter most for this proposal.

  • Campus builder programme. Visited five Kenyan universities and reached 503 developers. They produced 104 project ideas, and 23 submissions reached the hackerhouse. It showed us that the drop-off after ideas is the real problem, which this programme targets.

  • Pulse East Africa HackFest. Held in Kenya, Ethiopia, Rwanda, South Africa and Uganda, with at least 90 participants in each country.

  • CKB Builders Workshop, Kisumu (16 October 2026). 70 RSVPs, 37 attendees and about 11 builders with laptops ready to build.

  • Anything and Everything CKB X Space (14 November 2026). A public session with CKB builders and community members, where the community’s interest in building on CKB showed.

  • Community. Ongoing builder community across Kenya and wider Africa through Umojaverse’s X account, events and campus presence.

What these taught us. Attendance does not predict shipping, so the programme rewards on-chain proof of use. People who build together ship more, so the programme includes a physical hackerhouse. Builders also need practical guidance on getting users, so half of the sessions teach startup building.

Proof of work.
